a692947f406514be: Microsoft Windows 11 26H2 has arrived, and, unfortunately, it's already picked up a known audio issue within weeks of release. The glitch also affects Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2, which share the same code branch. It relates to decoding AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio and can cause the application using the decoder to crash abruptly or fail to start at all. Identified after the September 22 Windows update, the issue mostly impacts older applications, according to Microsoft. "Many modern applications do not use Windows for this type of encoding and therefore will not encounter this issue. "The code component involved in this issue is most commonly used in legacy applications that still rely on Windows built-in audio decoding." In summary – if your app has the temerity to use Windows built-in audio decoding for AC-3, you might have a problem. If it includes its own audio decoding component, you should be okay. "Affected applications may vary," explained Microsoft, "and can include games, media players, and certain productivity applications." There's also no fix as yet, so uninstalling is the only way to address it for now. To be clear, the AC-3 malfunction is not specific to Windows 11 26H2; the update preceded the release of the operating system's latest version by a week. It joins other known issues in 26H2, including other ongoing audio woes that have lingered in the list despite workarounds being available from Microsoft Support for Business. Microsoft currently has no mitigation for the AC-3 bug and offers little comfort to affected users: "We are working on releasing a resolution for this issue in a future Windows update." Acknowledging the latest trouble continues a run of misfortune for Microsoft. September's Patch Tuesday resulted in an out-of-band update to deal with RDP and Hyper-V issues. The update did not, however, fix all the audio problems it introduced, and the September 22 preview update has compounded the situation. Microsoft did not provide a timeline for resolving the latest issue. ®

7b441ca2abc39395: Sam Altman-backed AI chip startup Volantis has a plan to break through the memory wall using light, and this time it's not just an IP play. Founded in 2022, the San Francisco-based startup is developing an AI accelerator that will use a photonic interposer to dramatically increase memory bandwidth without compromising on capacity. Volantis believes it can pack upwards of 10 TB of memory at speeds up to 240 TB/s onto a single massive package. This, it claims, should be enough to serve a 20 trillion parameter model at 10,000 tok/s per user. To do this, Volantis is taking a somewhat unusual approach. Rather than developing some novel compute architecture or memory technology, the company is focusing its efforts on the optical interposer. Everything else it plans to license from IP providers. "The differentiation is primarily coming from the optical interposer. So why don't we license absolutely everything we possibly can, even if it's not the highest performance in the world, because we're already biting off a lot of risk with the interposer and the integration," CEO Tapa Ghosh tells El Reg. The basic idea behind the chip, which Volantis is calling A-1, is that by using optical wave guides rather than electrical interconnects it can dramatically increase the amount of high-bandwidth memory per package. Because of the speeds at which most AI accelerator memory, like HBM, operate, and the size and number of data pins used, it needs to be as close to the compute as possible to minimize power consumption and maximize signal integrity. As a result the maximum capacity and bandwidth of modern GPUs is limited by the compute die's shoreline. That's the physical perimeter around the chip. For now, that means the cap is right around 432 GB on AMD's MI455X. Photonic interconnects can extend that much farther. Instead of a few millimeters the memory can be located a few centimeters away, eliminating the shoreline as a bottleneck. While HBM is useful as an example, we'll note Volantis hasn't said what memory tech its chip will use just yet. Volantis aims to achieve this using optical waveguides integrated into an interposer. Compute and memory designed or supplied by its partners will be packaged on top. If any of this sounds familiar, Volantis isn't the first to propose using silicon photonic interposers in this manner. As our sister site Next Platform has previously reported, both Lightmatter and Celestial AI have toyed with the idea in the past. In fact, we strongly suspect the idea of HBM-at-a-distance contributed to Marvell's decision to acquire Celestial for $5.5 billion. However, unlike either Celestial or Lightmatter, Volantis isn't trying to license its tech to other chipmakers. At least not yet. Instead it aims to develop a fully fledged inference chip. "It is, at least on day one, a way easier problem to demonstrate a solution that ships," Ghosh says. Another differentiator is the technology on which the startup's interposer is based. Rather than relying on external lasers, Volantis' design uses micro vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers — micro-VCSELs for short — and means the light source is integrated directly into the interposer. VCSELs aren't new by any means, but have faced criticism over their reliability. However, Volantis CTO Roy Meade tells us the technology has come a long way in recent years and by giving up some speed, significantly higher reliability can be achieved, a philosophy he describes as wide and efficient. "People are still constrained to this, what I would call a fat pipe point-to-point mentality, and naturally, if that's the case, you're going to go towards SerDes," he says. "If we were to go back and take a look at the benefits of a wide-and-efficient approach. HBM for example. Taking that same playbook makes a lot of sense." What Meade is getting at is that interconnects can achieve higher bandwidth in a couple different ways. The first is by increasing the link speed, and the second by using more links. For example an 800 Gbps link can be achieved using four 200 Gbps links or eight 100 Gbps links. In his example of HBM, higher bandwidth is achieved by using an extremely-wide bus but slower data rate per pin relative to other memory technologies. The same concept applies to Volantis' optical interposer-based accelerator. Power efficiency remains an open question that's dogged many photonics startups, but this may be less of a problem for Volantis because it's not trying to license its first-gen interposer tech. For its first product the company is targeting 1 picojoule per bit per 24 Gbps lane and a total system power of around 20kW. Volantis still has a ways to go before it tapes out its first production-ready chip, and will need to raise a fair bit more in venture capital to do that — far more than the $88 million it raised this week with the help of Lachy Groom, Abstract Ventures, and others. Ghosh is well aware of this. He says the funding will enable the company to scale from small-scale optical demonstrators to something more closely resembling the final product. The interposer alone is challenging enough, but then there is the complexity of actually integrating the IP they license. "Aggressively, we should aim for an MVP product in 12 to 18 months as our target," he tells us, noting that's to have a working prototype not volume production. ®

Heavy rain arrived about half an hour before the start time, delaying things significantly. 7106daef9061b8fe: BRASILIA: Right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro heads to an Oct 25 runoff election from a position of strength, riding a conservative wave that has left president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva facing a tough battle to win a fourth term.

In a surprise result that defied opinion polls, Bolsonaro won 56 million votes, finishing two percentage points ahead of the veteran leftist Lula and outperforming the first-round election results of his father, the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The 45-year-old Bolsonaro, who was little known until a few months ago, pitched himself as more "moderate" than his firebrand father, who is still revered among many on the right and whose legacy loomed large over the campaign.
Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to prevent Lula from taking power in 2023. His family and supporters believe he is the victim of political persecution.
The coup bid and a corruption probe against Flavio Bolsonaro did little to sway voters fed up with crime, violence and the battle to make ends meet in Latin America's biggest economy.
Flavio Bolsonaro has promised fiscal austerity in the face of rising public debt, a smaller state, lower taxes and a tougher crackdown on crime.
The Sao Paulo stock market opened 8% higher after the results, and the real strengthened against the dollar.
Bolsonaro's pitch to Brazilians echoes those that have won voters in Argentina, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Peru and Colombia, among others, who have elected right-wing presidents in recent years.
"The result was a vote for Bolsonarism and an anti-PT vote," political scientist Carolina Botelho of the Rio de Janeiro State University told AFP, referring to the president's Workers' Party.
"Lula still has a chance," she said, highlighting that since a return to democracy in 1989, every candidate leading in a first-round election has gone on to win Brazil's presidency.
Right doubles seats in Senate
Botelho said Lula will attempt to rally those who cast blank votes and the 33 million who abstained – representing 21% of registered voters.
The smaller candidates who garnered almost 8% of the vote are all right-leaning.
Bolsonaro won the most votes in Brazil's largest electoral strongholds: the states of Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais.

The surge of the right was also felt in Congress, where Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) nearly doubled its seats in the Senate. Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro won a seat in the upper house of Congress.
"The end of the era of Lula's Workers' Party has been decreed," a triumphant Flavio Bolsonaro declared on Sunday in Brasilia.
Aside from Jair Bolsonaro's presidency between 2019 and 2022, the PT has governed Brazil for around 20 years, mainly under Lula.

While Lula is revered for social programmes that have lifted millions out of poverty, he and the party remain haunted by massive corruption scandals, and promises to tackle problems like insecurity and organised crime that have expanded in recent years fell flat among jaded voters.
During Lula's third term in office, inflation has come under control, and unemployment fell to historic lows.
However, Brazilians complain about a loss of purchasing power, and authorities are concerned about rising household debt.
Extra time win?
But the 80-year-old has vowed to fight for what he says is a choice between democracy and the "barbarism" of the far right.
"I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people," Lula said Sunday.
Lula also rallied hard on the theme of Brazilian sovereignty in the face of pressure from US President Donald Trump, a Bolsonaro ally who has championed a swing to the right in Latin America.
Argentine President Javier Milei congratulated Flavio Bolsonaro on X regarding his lead over the "communist" Lula.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu wished Bolsonaro a "great victory" in the runoff election.

2ed77ae535f5ab3d: After adding text-based ads to its chatbot earlier this year, OpenAI announced on Monday that it was adding a new “visual ad format” to ChatGPT, which is precisely what it sounds like: Visual ads, like so much of the advertising content online, will now be part of the ChatGPT experience. OpenAI will initially test these ads during image generation. “Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy,” OpenAI explained. “For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.” If you build it, someone in the ‘States will inevitably find a way to cram an ad into it, which is why testing of OpenAI’s new ad format will begin sometime in October in the US, given its status as the advertising hellscape capital of the world. Visual ChatGPT ads will be initially tested during image generation in ChatGPT, though like much of the scheme it’s not particularly clear how that’ll work from OpenAI’s announcement. The company didn’t detail much of anything about the process, so ads might appear as a de facto loading screen while ChatGPT conjures up whatever visual slop users ask of it, or they might remain on screen after the image is generated. Or not - OpenAI told us it would have more to share once the ads enter testing. It’s also entirely unclear whether the ads will be generated by ChatGPT on the fly or pulled from a library of ads submitted by companies. OpenAI also didn’t say how it will target visual ads, which has one advertising firm CEO questioning whether the new format will be worth the expense for companies looking for captive eyeballs. "Search ads work because they meet people at the moment they're looking for something,” Donatas Smailys, CEO of creator marketing firm Billo, told The Register in an email. “Someone generating an image in ChatGPT is not shopping." OpenAI has explained how it matches ads to ChatGPT conversations, Smailys added, but given it hasn’t mentioned how it plans to target visual ads, he remains unconvinced that they’ll be an effective advertising tool. That, and they’ll be intrusive - it’s bad enough getting targeted text ads or being invited to chat with an advertising AI after clicking an ad - now visual clutter will be part of ChatGPT, too. Free users can opt out of ads without paying, but doing so disables tools including image generation; if you want to generate images without ads, Plus starts at $20 a month. ®

d2e4790c9fabcfed: For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions. Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions.

A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production. Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this. Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises. Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively.

The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold. First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge.

Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production. Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges.
The key findings include the following:

Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress. On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production. Even high-tech firms struggle with this. Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure.

Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success. A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics. This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate.

Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access. Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%). Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group).

Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents. Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents. The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this.

Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs. To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

1469bd84211a39cb: The age of LLM-assisted security vulnerability discovery is really starting to bite. Debian's latest Linux kernel security update comes with a formidable reading list of 1,313 CVE identifiers. The DSA-6528-1 Linux security advisory, published on September 29, covers kernel package version 6.12.111-1 for Debian 13, codenamed Trixie. Debian 13.7 was released on September 12, before upstream kernel 6.12.111 arrived nine days later. The Debian security tracker links to descriptions of the individual issues. We have not examined every entry. If we had, this article would not appear until after Debian 13.8 (which is likely to appear later in October), or possibly at some point in 2027. Several checked at random also affect older kernel versions, so the list should not be read as a tally of bugs introduced in 6.12.111. The Linux kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) in February 2024. Back in February this year, kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman described the Linux CVE assignment process in some detail. He said kernel development averages around nine changes an hour, with a feed of known bug fixes averaging about 30 changes a day providing the basis for the CNA team's review. The kernel team's policy is to assign CVEs automatically after fixes have reached a stable kernel tree. It takes a deliberately cautious approach because the security implications of a bug may not be apparent when it is fixed. A CVE identifier alone therefore says little about severity or exploitability. We strongly suspect that this number of CVEs is due to LLM bots doing the bug hunting, and quite possibly doing the bug fixing as well. Linux is not an anti-AI project, and neither is Debian. AI-assisted bug hunting is already swamping the Linux security mailing list, as The Register reported in May. Kroah-Hartman released kernel 6.12.112 on October 3. Its detailed changelog runs to more than 27,000 lines. With both the rates of change and the sizes of the changes getting so large, it is hard to deny that LLM bot assistance must be very useful to the hard-pressed maintainers. Whether coding bots constitute a net benefit to the projects, to software, or to humanity as a whole remains at best an open question. ®

10a9c3d442832f73: BRUSSELS: French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have urged the EU to develop a new legal arsenal to respond faster to any potential trade war with China, according to a letter seen by AFP on Monday.

While it stopped short of explicitly naming the Asian giant, the letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was sent just days before the EU trade commissioner heads to Beijing to tackle trade frictions.
"We need a credible instrument in the hands of the commission" for decisive action, including the ability to cut off access to the European single market "if needed", Macron and Merz wrote.
The proposed weapon could be deployed in a trade war, for example, if a country cut off supplies of critical raw materials.
If that happened, "the EU must be able to inflict damage comparable to that being done to us", a German government source said.
The US and China can retaliate faster and more robustly in any trade war, the source said, warning that the EU's tools were not "as effective".

Germany and France want to give the commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days. Under their proposal, such action would not need approval from the EU's 27 countries, though a weighted majority of states could block it.
Merz and Macron are expected to present their ideas at an EU leaders' summit next week in Brussels.
The new tool could be used against any country, but the EU's biggest trade concern is its deficit with China, which Brussels says is inflicting damage on key European sectors.

The commission is already working on new tools to protect its industries, with one option a European equivalent of "Section 301", the trade tool Washington has used to probe foreign practices it deems discriminatory, and retaliate with tariffs.
The EU's deficit in goods with China hit around €360 billion (around US$400 billion) last year, meaning the EU imported far from the Asian nation than it exported there.
European companies say they are undercut on prices by Chinese rivals in sectors ranging from steel for wind turbines to semiconductors and batteries.
Europe also depends heavily on Chinese supplies of critical raw materials.
Macron and Merz also want a new tool to reduce European dependencies.

824f32a545f4d149: FIFTY years after a student demonstration against dictatorship ended in a massacre, Thailand's latest generation of protesters say they still face threats. Nutthanit Duangmusit, 24, spent several months in pre-trial detention before being convicted under Thailand's strict royal defamation law, among almost 300 people charged under so-called lese majeste since 2020. She is on bail while she appeals against her conviction and has been helping organise commemorations for today's anniversary of the Oct 6, 1976 killings at Thammasat University.

In one of the darkest chapters in modern Thai history, security forces and right-wing mobs massacred student protesters at one of the nation's top universities. "Back then, guns were fired and bodies lay on the ground," Nutthanit said as she walked AFP through the campus in Bangkok. "Today, the violence comes through the law."

The crackdown followed the return of military dictator Thanom Kittikachorn, who was ousted three years earlier. Students gathered at Thammasat to oppose his return. At dawn on Oct 6, police and right-wing groups stormed the campus, shooting, beating and lynching protesters.

The official death toll was 46, but survivors and witnesses believe more than 100 were killed. Government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises said many of those involved in the incident have since died or could not be located.

The incident receives scant attention in Thai textbooks, leaving younger generations to learn about it from survivors and independent research. Nutthanit and her friends draw a clear line from 1976 to today, where the military is no longer in charge but conservative forces still wield significant influence.

She was involved in youth-led protests that began in 2020, which drew tens of thousands to demand democratic change and reform of the monarchy. In 2022, Nutthanit, then 20, and others polled Bangkok passersby about royal motorcades and the exercise of royal power. That and other political activities led to three convictions under lese majeste.

When many young protesters ended up in court, they were helped by lawyers, including Thammasat survivor Krisadang Nutcharut. Ahead of the anniversary, he expressed admiration for their courage and said a lese majeste reform was something "no one dares raise in my generation".

The protest movement has since subsided, with many activists imprisoned or fleeing abroad. The monarchy remains widely revered in Thailand, a largely traditionalist society where a conservative government was elected this year.

The memory of the massacre still triggers strong emotions on the other side. Chalermchai Majchaklam, now 73, was a vocational student at a rival institution who fought against the protesters. He accused the Thammasat students of attacking police and others from his institution, and said he believed they were trying to overthrow the monarchy. "We were there because we love the monarchy and we were angry," he said, adding that he would do it again.

Thiraphop Tengprawat, 21, was charged with lese majeste over a satirical banner displayed on another Thammasat campus last October after the university cancelled student events following the death of Queen Sirikit, the current king's mother. Police alleged the banner insulted Sirikit. "The problems we face today have a history," said Thiraphop, who is still waiting to hear if he will face trial.

The military seized power on the evening of the massacre and increased the punishment for royal defamation 15 days later. "The version of lese majeste enforced today is a legacy of that coup," said reform campaigner Nasree Phumkuea, 23.

Recent attempts to amend the lese majeste law have landed dozens of former and current members of parliament in court. For Nutthanit, the battle is increasingly personal. In May 2024, her close friend Netiporn Sanesangkhom died in custody following a prolonged hunger strike. She was 28.
"Fifty years later, people are still dying for justice or being forced into exile," Nutthanit said. "It feels as though Thailand keeps returning to the same place."

1264e88e3a156703: WHAT'S more volatile than President Donald Trump? The answer may be a lame duck Donald Trump after the United States midterm elections. The 80-year-old billionaire faces a bruising final two years in the White House if Republicans lose control of Congress in the Nov 3 polls amid voter anger over the Iran war and soaring prices. Investigations and a possible third impeachment would loom as his Democratic foes seek revenge. The president who loves to boast of his power would find much of it stymied.

But Trump with his back to the wall could cause major upheaval, from revenge at home to wars abroad — and influencing the race to be his successor in 2028. "I don't think he is going to go out with a whimper, he's going to try to go out with a bang," said Allan Lichtman, a professor at American University and author of Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation. "He can't stand not being the centre of attention. So this may spark him to be even more aggressive."
US presidents are often punished in midterm elections, weakening their party in Congress and leaving them with the dreaded lame duck epithet as their power wanes towards the end.

But if Republicans lose the House of Representatives as expected —and possibly the Senate too —Trump will find himself in a precarious position as Democrats probe alleged corruption or abuse of power. He has already signalled he will take his usual combative approach. "They'll probably go after me, and I'll go after them," Trump said in a Time Magazine interview published this week. "I think he's going to be in attack mode," said Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution.

First of all, Trump baselessly disputed his 2020 presidential election loss to Joe Biden and it is "entirely possible" he could claim irregularities in the midterms as well, said Hass. Then, Trump could direct the Department of Justice to investigate leading Democrats probing him, in the same way that a number of his opponents have found themselves facing legal action.

In the longer term, Trump sometimes hints at running for a constitutionally-barred third term in the White House, even wearing a "Trump 2028" hat at a gala media dinner in July. Lichtman said talk of a third term was to "stay relevant", but added that Trump would "keep the focus on himself by being the kingmaker" for the Republican nomination.

Trump —who hosted the television show The Apprentice in which he uttered the catchphrase "you're fired" — has been coy about backing either Vice-President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the top job. "I assume he'll want to keep the suspense," said Hass. "Who's going to watch the show if it's already been predetermined who's the winner?"

Outgoing US presidents have often doubled down on foreign policy in the waning days of their terms, as it's the area in which they have the most power. Trump said he may resume bombing Iran after the midterms, but prolonging a quagmire that his MAGA base hates could be politically and militarily risky. "You could make the argument that he'll let it rip, but I don't think he wants his legacy to be a warmonger. "He wants his legacy to have left America stronger," said Hass, who served in the National Security Council under president Barack Obama.

Hass expected Trump to continue the US pullback from some of its western allies while maintaining detente with authoritarian Russia and China and keeping a focus on Latin America. On trade, however, Trump would likely remain "unrelentingly active", as shown by his recent hostility towards Canada, Hass said.

Trump, like many other soon-to-be retirees, ultimately may be more interested in a little home improvement. The real estate tycoon appears increasingly obsessed by his construction projects at the White House, such as his new ballroom and helipad. For Trump, stamping his mark on Washington in granite and concrete may be the greatest legacy of all.
"I love doing it," Trump said during a recent event at the White House, "because that's what I did my whole life."

3b9adb7b13ade5fd: It is ironic that while schools and hostels are meant to protect students, some of the gravest dangers can come from within.

Last month, a 14-year-old boy died after being found unconscious at a school hostel in Kuala Pilah, with police investigating an alleged assault. On Saturday, a 16-year-old schoolgirl was found dead in a school hall in Yong Peng, and three male schoolmates have been detained in connection with her death.

These tragedies are a grim reminder that schools and hostels, which should be safe places for children, are not immune to violence. Between 2021 and 2026, Malaysia has seen a disturbing series of bullying and assault cases involving students.
The Education Ministry's Student Discipline System recorded 21,307 bullying cases between 2021 and 2025.

The numbers alone are cause for concern. But repeated cases of violence raise a more fundamental question: are existing safeguards enough to protect students from threats within the school community? This is not to suggest that every incident has the same cause.

Bullying, hazing, peer violence and failures of supervision can have different causes. What they have in common is the potential to escalate when warning signs are missed, complaints are ignored or supervision fails.

In boarding schools, an entrenched culture of seniority can foster intimidation, hazing and peer-enforced punishment, sometimes normalised as a "rite of passage". Serious incidents must never be treated as mere disciplinary matters.
The Education Ministry's order for a comprehensive review, with instructions "not to hide anything", is therefore welcome.
But investigations after tragedies are not enough. What is needed is a systematic review of how schools identify risks, respond to complaints and protect students before violence occurs.
School safety measures and safeguards must therefore be thoroughly reviewed.
While each tragedy is different, repeated incidents should compel authorities to strengthen prevention, supervision and emergency responses.
This should include safety audits of schools, checks on CCTV coverage and blind spots, stronger access controls, attendance monitoring and closer supervision of students.

The education minister's latest directive must be translated into concrete action. Risks within schools and hostels must be identified early, with clear channels for students to report bullying, suspicious behaviour and threats before they escalate.
Schools must remain places of learning and safety, not places where violence is allowed to become normal.

bdb94ac49743a198: Today, I’m talking with Sen. Adam Schiff, a Democrat from California. Schiff sits on a number of committees with oversight into tech and AI: intellectual property, antitrust, privacy and technology — it’s all there. I really wanted to ask him about how we might regulate anything related to the tech industry at this moment in time.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

But as you’ll hear, he started our conversation by talking about the self-dealing and corruption present all through our politics. That of course fell against the backdrop of President Donald Trump gathering AI CEOs to the White House to sign a nonbinding pact in which they agree to, you know, do a good job keeping AI safe.

I asked Schiff if he thinks that’s enough, how he thinks a more formal regulatory framework would look, and what might happen next if Democrats retake Congress in the midterms — all the way to whether he’d support impeaching the president (again) over all that corruption. We also spent some time comparing and contrasting how you might regulate AI with where we’ve landed regulating social media.

One nerdy note: You’re going to hear me ask the senator about something called Chevron deference and a Supreme Court case called Loper Bright. Basically, the Supreme Court overturned a Reagan-era precedent saying courts would defer to experts in agencies when the law was vague.

Now, the courts get to decide, which could cause any new regulation to get immediately tied up in litigation. That seems awfully relevant to the idea of creating a new agency to regulate AI, which Schiff supports doing.
Okay: California Sen. Adam Schiff. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Sen. Adam Schiff, you’re a United States senator from California. Welcome to Decoder.
Thank you. Great to be with you.
I have been asking every politician who comes on the show this very basic question here in 2026. Senator, what the hell is going on in our country?

It’s a very good question. I think we have seen things take place in the last couple of years in particular that we’ve never seen before. There’s sadly rampant corruption within the administration. Every day, every week, it’s a new thing. At the moment, I think what is most jarring is seeing campaign ads aired of the president that are paid for by taxpayer dollars. But every week it’s something else. It’s excluding press from the White House or Air Force One, or it’s some new moneymaking scheme or some new vanity project. If you look at, for example, the triumphal arch, they’re now claiming it’s a national security issue because they want to store ammunition in it. And why do they want to do that? Because the best legal argument they have is that this is not just cosmetic, that they have some national security purpose.

So what are we seeing in the country? We’re seeing chaos and no focus on the cost of living and improving the quality of people’s lives at the administration level, or by my Republican colleagues in Congress, but I’m hoping that changes.

The national security piece is very interesting to me in the context of a bunch of questions I have for you, because the Trump administration loves to justify every single thing it does by saying it’s national security, and it can’t be questioned, and this should bring more authority to the executive branch in one way or another. And they’ve been doing that since the beginning.

But just this week, we had a bunch of tech executives at the White House signing a non-binding promise to evaluate their own AI systems. And there was no national security concern that made any of that binding, even though they are among the most prominent people in the country saying they might kill everyone. Can you square that circle at all?

It’s very hard to square. It was interesting to see all those tech leaders there signing onto this voluntary pledge on the one hand and on the other hand, away from the White House grounds, away from the president, being very public and saying, “We need regulation. We don’t want this to be just ‘Trust us, we’ll do the right thing.’” So yeah, it was very distant, very jarring. None of these companies want to incur the wrath of this very vengeful president. Apparently, they will say what he wants them to say in his presence. But the reality is, there is a real national security threat here. As these models become more and more advanced, as they advance themselves through this recursive AI, we have less and less of a sense of what they’re doing, how they’re deciding what they’re deciding, and what they’re trying to access lawfully or unlawfully.

That is a national security concern of the highest order. There are other security concerns too. The unbridled implementation of AI at the Pentagon can result in calamities, and we need to investigate what role AI may have played in target selection in the bombing of that Iranian girls’ school, for example. There has been an effort to go after Anthropic, because Anthropic wanted to insist on not using AI for domestic mass surveillance or for fully autonomous weapons systems. That’s a national security issue. And their response in the administration was to try to kill Anthropic, and they’re still at it. So lots of national security concerns, none of them aired.

When the president was asked about this by a reporter, he said, “Well, the world doesn’t have to worry about this because these companies love America.” I’m not really sure that’s much of an answer. And when he was asked, “Well, isn’t there anything else that’s necessary?” He pointed to his brain and wanted people to take comfort that he has, I guess, a very big brain, he tells us. He’s a stable genius, and therefore we don’t need to worry.
He’s passed all the tests. So I’ve been told.

You are obviously on a number of committees, but most importantly, I think for this conversation, you’re on a number of subcommittees as part of the Senate Judiciary Committee that are in the strike zone for AI. So you’re the ranking member on the subcommittee on Intellectual Property, you’re on the Privacy, Technology and the Law subcommittee, and then, of course, the Antitrust Competition Policy and Consumer Rights Committee. I just look at that list, and that is the dead center of the AI regulatory debate.

What’s the conversation in Congress like as you debate these issues? In particular, I look at the IP issues, and they seem existential to these companies. If we start charging them for training data, they might not exist anymore.

I think that’s right. When you look at, for example, all of the IP that’s been vacuumed up by these models to train these models, that’s a lot of the value of some of these entertainment companies. And so they live or die on the strength of their IP. But what makes this challenging is that not all of the players in the industry are the same. You’ve got big streamers involved; you’ve got big technology companies involved. You’ve got companies whose AI or their technology portfolio is much more important to them than the IP value of their film library. I don’t think the film library at Amazon is Amazon’s most important business. If it was, they probably wouldn’t have made the movie Melania. But my favorite review of that, by the way, was the Variety reviewer who said, “If you watch that movie on a plane, you would still walk out.”

But the IP issues are really important. Senator Curtis and I are working together on them to begin by saying, we want to know what copyrighted material, what protected material, was used to train these models. And then we can have a discussion about what’s fair use and what isn’t, but we need these companies to retain that information. But lots of other IP issues, some beneficial. We had a hearing on the patent office, and the patent office’s use of AI to more quickly get through the backlog of patent applications. So there are going to be good applications too in the IP area, but also a lot of worry about what it means for people’s creative talents.

I wanted to start with IP, not just because I’m a failed former copyright lawyer myself, and emphasis on the failed. I was no good at it. But it just seems like what this industry needs right now is a pretty holistic approach to regulation. So are the inputs of the models being collected in a legal way that benefits the ecosystem that created them? Are the studios going to get paid for a bunch of training data? Are website operators going to get paid for training Google’s models that they scrape with search? And then you’re on to, do they need an antitrust exemption so they can coordinate on safety and they don’t kill us all? And there’s a whole list of things in between those two ideas that also need some regulatory frameworks, that might just need some basic transparency laws.
What do you think about that? Is our government prepared to start at the beginning, and end at the end, and do all the steps in the middle?

Well, how I think about it is you’ve got all the input issues, and it really seems like the thought at these companies was, “We’re in a race. We’re just going to vacuum it all up. And yes, this probably violates a lot of the IP laws, but if we don’t do it, the other companies are going to do it. We’ll worry about the legality later.” So that’s what they’ve done. And of course they’re being sued by different parties, and some are settling these cases, and some are fighting these cases. But they began the process by just deciding they were going to ignore IP law, and they were just going to take [IP] and worry about the problems later.

And then, in terms of the outputs, it has taken us to where we are today for these companies, I think, to consider the safety of the outputs. Do we need to start slowing down the pace of our development of these models because we don’t trust the outputs? We don’t know where they’ll lead. We can’t even control these models ourselves, let alone provide these models to the public, to good actors, to bad actors, and expect that we’re not going to have some terrible result. In terms of how I think about this holistically as a legislator, this is crying out for legislation. I am, I’ll be honest, very circumspect about Congress and legislating the tech sector because we did such a — I don’t know what language I’m allowed to use here — but such a shitty job when it comes to any kind of regulation of the harms, the societal harms coming out of social media.

We’re going to have to do a much better job and much more quickly when it comes to AI, because the threats are even more significant and we’re already at the point of strong potential harms. It can’t wait. We certainly can’t take the kind of years we’ve taken to try to even wrap ourselves around social media.

Can I ask about that comparison? I hear it a lot. I hear it from politicians. I hear it from the industry itself. I hear it from parents, of course. It seems to me that the problem with social media regulation was never that we’re too slow, or that no one can come up with an idea; it was always the very existence of the First Amendment. The thing you needed to do with social media was regulate the flow of disinformation, or keep teens from bullying one another, or from posting pro-anorexia content.

All of that came down to being speech regulation. The companies knew this; the tech companies absolutely knew this. And I remember they would put up billboards in DC. Meta would put up billboards saying, “We welcome regulation.” Then I would listen to the ideas for regulation, and they would crash headfirst into the First Amendment, and then nothing would happen.

And it seemed like that paralyzed us from doing things like privacy regulation, because it was tied up next to the very idea of social media. It doesn’t feel that way with AI. Do you and your peers in Congress draw the distinction that it isn’t the First Amendment preventing you from doing a lot of the things that you might do for social media, in the AI case?

Honestly, I don’t think it was the First Amendment that was the issue in regulating social media. I think the First Amendment was certainly used by companies that didn’t want regulation to try to argue everything was a First Amendment issue, when so much wasn’t a First Amendment issue. The threshold question in terms of regulation of the social media companies is: is the broad immunity they have under Section 230 still working? The industry asked for that one-size-doesn’t-fit-all immunity because it said, “We’re a nascent industry, don’t regulate us, don’t inhibit us. If you try to regulate us, then we will feel, or if we’re not immune, that it’s necessary to take down content because we might get sued over it. We want to be good actors. We want to take down offensive conduct, but we don’t want to get sued for that either. So give us carte blanche.”

And they got it. They got carte blanche, and they have not been good citizens, corporate citizens, and they’ve allowed a lot of harm to take place, and they’ve trained their algorithms for addiction. So much of the content has been harmful to young people, and so much of the content has violated their own policies, but they have been immune from any consequences because of the breadth of what Congress gave them. Now they found it, I think, strategically, a good strategy is to frame these things as the First Amendment, and to attack the other side and say, “Oh, there’s a bias that is against conservatives,” or whatever. It was all in the service of keeping that unregulated.

So I really don’t think the First Amendment has been the issue, but I think it has been utilized as a bludgeon to try to stop any kind of meaningful regulation. I similarly worry that all of the money around AI may result in the same paralysis if members of Congress aren’t willing to do the right thing, and aren’t willing to put in place safeguards regardless of how much different industry players might spend.

We’ve had Sen. [Ron] Wyden on the show many times to talk about Section 230. I won’t go too far down that rabbit hole. The dynamic there was that Section 230 provided the immunity that you’re describing, but it was immunity for speech that would otherwise be illegal. And so it was speech that was defamatory. There’s a whole category of speech that isn’t illegal. Are you saying that taking the 230 immunity away from the social platforms would somehow make them moderate lawful but awful speech? And I bring this up because I’m very curious about how you would apply it in the AI case as well.

Yeah, no, I think that is the case. That part of their argument was, ” We want to take down really nasty, offensive, racist content, but we will be afraid to do so if you don’t give us immunity. So give us immunity, and we’ll take all that bad stuff down.” They got immunity. And I don’t know if you’ve been on X lately; it’s a cesspool. So giving them broad immunity did not allow them to enforce their community policies. And the First Amendment prohibits the government from dictating speech or prohibiting you from saying things. It doesn’t prohibit a private party from saying, “We don’t want racist content on our platform.” So there’s no problem with a private platform saying, “That violates our policy. We’re not going to post it.” And they’re not utilizing that immunity in a good way. So why should they continue to have it?

Now, we may want to create a safe harbor for companies that are meeting best practices and standards. So we may want to narrow 230 instead of getting rid of it. What is the analogy in terms of AI? I’m not sure what the analogy is.

Let me draw you the connection that I’ve been thinking about a lot. In the case of social media and Section 230, the immunity was that the platforms would not be responsible for the speech of the users. So I would post something horrible about you, and you couldn’t sue Mark Zuckerberg. This is the thing that has broadly enabled the social media platforms at scale.

I opened Instagram today, and it is all but making the content for me. And in fact, a lot of content on Instagram is being generated by Meta. It is obviously their speech. And somewhere between having your Muse go and make Instagram for you, and Meta synthesizing all of the product recommendations and generating content all by itself, is a liability for Meta. It is outside of the Section 230 shield. That is their speech.

And you can draw a lot of distinctions there. If I fully automate my Instagram account with my Meta agent, is that my speech, Meta speech, or the AI model’s speech? Who knows? But it might not be under 230. So you would be outside of the immunity shield. And I’m just curious if you think that will meaningfully alter how they moderate.

I agree with your analysis, but I think it’s a difficult enough legal analysis that they feel they’ve got the money to stop, or slow down, effective litigation. Meta, or any of these other companies, decides how they want to amplify certain content. So let’s say it’s content that I generated. Is it still solely my speech if Meta spends a fortune to amplify it to so many users who wouldn’t have heard it, but for Meta making that decision, or is it now both of our speech? I’m not sure exactly where that line is. If it’s obviously purely Meta content, then it’s pretty simple, but there are going to be a lot of cases in between.

But I think the broader question is: is 230 in its current form still meeting its purpose? I don’t think it is, but I know there’s no consensus over what that ought to look like. And that is part of what has hampered us from doing anything. But even the smallish stuff, the small-bore stuff like don’t allow your platforms to encourage people to commit suicide has been hard for us to do in the social media context. Really, litigation has been more effective than legislation because we haven’t been able to legislate. If you look now to AI, we made some progress legislatively, at least in terms of the process in trying to prevent AI chatbots from telling kids how to commit suicide or keep it from their parents. But even those little things are still not at the finish line. So what does that say about our capacity to do the big things?
Historically, when stuff is tough like this, we wait for calamity. And in the case of AI, because that calamity could be just massive, we can’t afford to do that.

It does seem to me like we’re about to run a fairly large-scale A/B test on the value of the 230 immunity. Whatever ChatGPT is saying to people is very clearly OpenAI speech. And then somewhere next to that is the kind of clarification law that AI companies are talking about in terms of agents and things like the Hugging Face attack, where they don’t know if a user directing an agent to do something bad is their fault. Whether that liability should pass through them if I’m the person who told my agent to go do some horrible hacking attack.

I talked to the tech industry, and the thing they want from legislation is actual clarity in the law. And instead, what we’ve gotten is this non-binding agreement with the Trump administration that simply says things like, “The companies will empower an internal team to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended,” which feels like nothing. To me, that is literally meaningless. Does that strike you as toothless and as meaningless as it does to me?

Yeah, it certainly does. I think it really is meaningless. I’ve been thinking about the question you just raised. It’s interesting that you brought that up, and that is: where does the legal liability rest today? So if you have these bots hacking into Australian websites, or you have them hacking into Hugging Face, clearly that is the responsibility of these models because that’s not being done at the behest of one of their customers.

cc0cc73028fcaa45: MOSCOW: Moscow on Monday downplayed reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, stressing that post-mortem tests had not detected the disease, while Washington said it was closely monitoring the situation.
Reports on Friday that plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
The news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said she may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
But Irkutsk regional governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".

He said on Telegram that Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had determined, following tests, that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".
He added that there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the woman's death.
Kobzev said the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "stable".
"The situation remains under our control and that of the experts."
Asked about the situation on Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements rather than ... rumours and speculations".

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, the most contagious type. Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said his country was monitoring the situation but saw no "cause for alarm".

"There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread," Rubio told reporters before taking off for a visit to Iceland.
"So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we're doing that."
25576fda11d2fbb4: MOSCOW: A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia has fallen ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people, and the head of Russia's health watchdog to fly to the Irkutsk region.
The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said on Monday the situation was under control.

Plague is endemic to Siberia, location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas. It is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, though cases in other parts of the world - notably Africa - occur every year.
Local media named the woman as Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
There were conflicting reports about how and where the laboratory worker, whose age was given as 28, had fallen ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia of as-yet unestablished origin.
AUTHORITIES SAY NO NEW CASES REPORTED, ALL CONTACTS TRACED

Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, told state media the institute had not found evidence of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens after rumours spread on social media that the woman had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria.
Nevertheless, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Siberia for an emergency meeting over the weekend.

An unspecified number of people who had been in contact with the dead woman were quarantined, parts of the hospital in the town of Shelekhov where she died were cordoned off, and an aluminium plant told its workers to wear masks.
Authorities urged people to remain calm and said there was no evidence that the woman's death was linked to her work.

Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement that she had died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", adding: "Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified."
He said the situation was under control and that all known contacts of the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.
Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, prompts the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
If identified quickly, it can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days.

564c8cd99d191ccc: KUALA LUMPUR: The investigation papers on the incident involving Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain will be handed over to the Attorney-General's Chambers tomorrow.

Khalid said investigations began when two policemen lodged reports claiming they were physically manhandled by Shuhaily at Kuala Lumpur International Airport on Sept 28.
He said federal police Criminal Investigation Department investigators launched a probe under Section 323 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt.
"The investigation was conducted transparently, professionally and impartially, based on witness statements and evidence obtained to ensure every aspect of the incident is thoroughly examined.
"A conviction under Section 323 of the Penal Code carries a maximum prison sentence of a year, or a fine of up to RM2,000, or both," he said.
Khalid said people should not speculate on the incident, nor should they draw any conclusions, as these could jeopardise the investigation.

Previously, a video showing Shuhaily during an incident at KLIA Terminal 1 went viral on social media following an MCBA operation with a Aviation Security (AvSec) team against the activities of foreign touts at the airport.
Shuhaily later explained that a foreigner had been taken to the AvSec baggage inspection room before two individuals entered the area and recorded the incident.
He left it to the police to conduct further investigations into the incident and said he was prepared to accept any decision made by the government regarding the matter.

fff9fbcac1b926e8: PETALING JAYA: Former Umno information chief Shahril Hamdan has questioned whether an April 19 proclamation on the removal of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan could be considered valid after it was signed by menteri besar Ismail Lasim months later.
Shahril questioned whether a document, initially issued without the menteri besar’s signature, could be held until a new menteri besar took office and signed it.
“It’s like backdating it,” he said on the latest episode of the Keluar Sekejap podcast.
Shahril acknowledged that he was unsure of the legal position but said there could be grounds to argue that such a process was not permissible.
“That is a legal question I’m not too sure about, but I think there is an argument that says it cannot be done that way.
“If they still want to remove him, then start a new process, issue a new proclamation under the current menteri besar and the current undangs,” he said.
Muda deputy president Zaidel Baharuddin similarly questioned why the parties involved continued to rely on the April 19 proclamation instead of starting a fresh process.
“Why must we look at April 19? Why not start a new process and correct it from the beginning?
“Once that dispute is resolved ... then start a new process with the new undangs.”
Ismail took his oath of office and pledged allegiance as menteri besar before Tuanku Muhriz on Aug 2, before signing the proclamation the following day.
He later said he had signed it under duress and lodged a police report over the matter. He also maintained that the document was invalid as it did not comply with the Negeri Sembilan constitution.
A week later, however, he endorsed a statement by his 10 executive council members purportedly affirming Tuanku Muhriz’s removal as ruler.

“Over the past two years, we have frequently told people that universities are not the only place for them to pursue their studies.
“We also have other institutions, such as polytechnics and community colleges, that offer skills certificates in technical and vocational education and training.

“For years, society has viewed polytechnics as a second choice for those who cannot get into university, but now applications to enter polytechnics have reached 132%, compared with 60% to 70% previously,” Bernama quoted him as saying at a dialogue at Angkasapuri today.

Zambry said technical and engineering fields did not depend solely on degree qualifications, but also required skilled workers who had undergone engineering-related training at institutions offering training in various skills.
11076c8ef141f0d8: ALOR SETAR: The Kedah Ministry of Domestic Trade and Costs of Living has taken RON95 petrol samples from 11 petrol stations in several districts for analysis following recent viral claims that the fuel was mixed with water.
State director Muhammad Nizam Jamaludin said the action followed public complaints that vehicles had broken down after refuelling at the affected stations.
"Ministry enforcement teams conducted inspections at 11 petrol stations today and took fuel samples from the involved tanks or pumps for inspection and further analysis.

"At the same time, preliminary inspections using the manual dipping method and a review of the Automatic Tank Gauge (ATG) system readings showed no indication of the presence of water in the inspected fuel storage tanks," he said in a statement today.
He said the inspections covered Petron and Caltex stations in Alor Setar, Kubang Pasu, Sungai Petani and Kulim, as well as checks of fuel supply receipts, sales records and other relevant documents.

However, Muhammad Nizam said the preliminary findings were not conclusive, adding that the samples would be sent to the Department of Chemistry for analysis while the operators would also send samples to their respective oil companies' laboratories.

"The ministry will scrutinise the analysis results and the overall investigation findings before determining the next course of action, including taking appropriate measures if there is any violation of legal provisions," he said.
Members of the public can channel complaints via WhatsApp at 019-848 8000, the KPDN e-Aduan portal, the KPDN Call Centre at 1-800-886-800 or the KPDN EzADU smartphone application.
d2261e1bac3ba157: KUALA LUMPUR: Zetrix AI Bhd has submitted a proposal to the government to resolve outstanding remittances following the suspension of its Road Transport Department (RTD) services from today.
In its statement today, Zetrix AI said its immediate priority is to resolve the outstanding obligations and work towards restoring the affected services, subject to necessary government approvals.
"Zetrix AI has submitted a proposed solution to the government of Malaysia to address the outstanding remittances for its consideration," it said.
The company did not disclose details of the proposal or the amount involved.

The move comes as the company faces RM314 million in outstanding government revenue collections, with Transport Minister Anthony Loke clarifying today that the amount relates to collections made between May 19 and Sept 30 this year.
Loke said the arrears were not accumulated over three years, as reported earlier, but had built up over several months.
The ministry and RTD reportedly had issued 35 reminders and held four engagement sessions with the company and other stakeholders to recover the money.
The issue came to wider attention last week when reports said Zetrix, formerly known as MyEG Services Bhd, owed the government more than RM200 million in unremitted collections.

The Straits Times, citing official documents and a government source, reported on Oct 2 that the amount had exceeded RM200 million by end-September and involved collections from road tax renewals, driving licences and traffic summonses.
However, Loke's latest clarification puts the outstanding amount at RM314 million and said the arrears covered the period from May 19 to Sept 30.
Loke also reportedly said the company submitted a post-dated cheque for RM231 million dated Sept 30, but the bank did not process the payment following instructions from the company.
The government subsequently suspended RTD payment services through MyEG and Zetrix AI effective Oct 5.

Zetrix AI, through the MyEG business, has been an RTD collection agent since 2000, handling services including motor vehicle licence renewals, vehicle ownership transfers, driving licence services and electronic summons payments.
Collection agents must remit government revenue within one working day of each transaction.
Zetrix AI said it regretted the inconvenience caused to customers and assured those who accessed affected RTD services before the suspension that their transactions had been processed and fulfilled.
It said further updates would be provided once information was confirmed.
acd789e6234ad43f: PETALING JAYA: Pihak berkuasa sepatutnya sudah menjangkakan masalah pengangkutan yang menyebabkan puluhan ribu peminat Formula Satu (F1) terkandas ketika Grand Prix (GP) Bahrain berlangsung di Litar Antarabangsa Sepang (SIC) hujung minggu lepas, kata Shahril Hamdan.
Shahril mengakui situasi itu agak luar biasa memandangkan Malaysia hanyalah tuan rumah, manakala penganjurnya ialah Litar Antarabangsa Bahrain (BIC).
Bagaimanapun, katanya, pengunjung antarabangsa tetap akan mengaitkan pengalaman buruk itu dengan imej negara.
Justeru, beliau menyarankan Malaysia mempertimbangkan syarat lebih ketat terhadap penganjur pada masa depan demi memastikan kemudahan pengangkutan mencukupi sekali gus menjaga reputasi negara.
“Saya juga ada rasa sedikit 'frust' kerana kenapa tidak pihak kita, pihak di peringkat Malaysia ini, sama ada SIC atau Rapid KL dapat jangkakan benda ini akan berlaku.
"Orang luar tak fikir ini Bahrain (anjurkan) ke apa. Mereka marah Malaysia, dan tak berapa cantiklah bagi imej kita," kata ketua penerangan Umno itu dalam episod terbaru audio siar Keluar Sekejap.

Perlumbaan F1 hujung minggu lepas merupakan yang pertama diadakan di Sepang sejak GP Malaysia dihentikan pada 2017 selepas 18 tahun penganjuran, ekoran kos yang kian meningkat serta pulangan yang merosot.
Pengunjung mula mengkritik SIC sejak Jumaat lepas susulan kesesakan teruk serta masa menunggu yang terlalu lama bagi perkhidmatan bas perantara ke kawasan parkir dan hab pengangkutan berhampiran.

Peminat turut mengadu tentang kelewatan ketika keluar masuk litar, manakala pengguna media sosial mendakwa orang ramai terpaksa berjalan kaki di lorong kecemasan lebuh raya sementara menanti ketibaan bas.
Kesesakan luar biasa turut dilaporkan di sekitar litar dan laluan menghala ke Kuala Lumpur serta lapangan terbang sejurus perlumbaan berakhir pada Ahad.
Timbalan Presiden Muda Zaidel Baharuddin, yang hadir selaku hos jemputan bersama dalam audio siar itu, berpandangan masih terlalu awal untuk menyalahkan mana-mana pihak di Malaysia.
Menurut Zaidel, SIC sebelum ini berpengalaman mengendalikan kehadiran penonton berskala besar bagi acara MotoGP tanpa masalah sedemikian.
Beliau bagaimanapun tidak menyentuh mengenai penganjuran GP Bahrain selama tiga hari itu yang menarik kehadiran luar biasa lebih 200,000 peminat sukan permotoran.
Menurut Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif BIC Sheikh Salman Isa Al Khalifa, rekod 261,000 penonton hadir sepanjang acara berlangsung, termasuk 103,000 orang pada hari kemuncak perlumbaan pada Ahad.
fb2fad77f94f82fe: PETALING JAYA: The investigation paper into an allegation that Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) director-general Shuhaily Zain assaulted two police personnel at KLIA will be submitted to the Attorney-General’s Chambers tomorrow.

Inspector-General of Police Khalid Ismail said police had recorded statements from 25 witnesses, including police and AKPS personnel, Malaysia Airports auxiliary police, baggage handlers, medical officers, and members of the public.
“All aspects of the incident will be examined before the investigation paper is referred to the AGC tomorrow for further instructions,” he said in a statement.
Khalid said the case is being investigated by Bukit Aman’s criminal investigation department under Section 323 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt.
The offence carries a maximum jail term of one year, a fine of up to RM2,000, or both, upon conviction.
Khalid said the investigation was being conducted “transparently, professionally and impartially”, based on witness statements and other evidence gathered.
The case came to public attention after CCTV footage allegedly showing Shuhaily confronting an individual at KLIA Terminal 1 went viral.
AKPS later confirmed the footage was genuine and said the incident occurred while Shuhaily was inspecting preparations at KLIA ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
The agency said its officers were also conducting an operation against foreign touts at the airport.
Shuhaily has said he would cooperate with the investigation and accept whatever decision is made by the authorities.
e399a779075fdb58: Games Workshop is on the hunt for a head of IT to guide the organization through its technological saga for the next two years. The UK-based tabletop games retailer and manufacturer of the globally popular Warhammer figures said that under the fixed-term contract, the heroic individual would take overall responsibility for its global IT and customer technology capability, and report to the Chief Operating Officer. “The role has a broad remit spanning our core technology estate, information security, major systems change and the technology behind our customer-facing digital platforms, including warhammer.com,” the job ad said, although sadly it closed for applications over the weekend. “We need someone who can understand what Games Workshop needs now, anticipate what we will need in the future, and make good decisions about how technology supports the long-term success of the business,” it said. Candidates might want to be aware that, if they are lucky enough to be offered the job and they accept the mission, the battle will not be an easy one. The head of IT will take responsibility for core IT environment and information security, advising senior management on technology, security, risk and investment. They will also support the teams to keep “significant technology programs moving, openly tackling the challenges that come with major change, and ensure that we continue to make rapid progress.” The Nottingham-based retailer and manufacturer is in the midst of ERP and supply chain management systems overhauls that were first mobilized years ago and have been beset with delays and over-runs. Back in January 2021, The Register reported that Games Workshop delayed its Microsoft Dynamics-based ERP rollout and appointed a new integrator, having already hoped to go live in 2020. By September that year, it said project issues were impacting the development of new features in online shopping. In January 2022, it added another £500k to the project budget with no end in sight. A year later, it said the business faced ongoing challenges to integrate new IT systems when it was still heavily reliant on working with its legacy tech systems. “Finishing these projects and upgrading our systems continue to be a key area of focus. We are making some progress but it's costing us more time and money – we will remain cost conscious," it told investors. Around four years later, challenges remain ongoing, according to the latest annual report, published in July, for the year ending in May 2026. It said the group’s main financial system is still being supported by a number of legacy ERP applications for which “we have identified control deficiencies in our previous audits.” These still exist, according to a review of IT systems. The report added that the responsibility for delivering IT had moved to its operational manufacturing and supply chain director, under the COO from June, a decision which “helped bring all of the internal departments together.” “Our Systems Improvement Plan (SIP) is on track with very clear milestones for us all to support and deliver,” it added. Games Workshop is famous for the phenomenon of Warhammer 40,000 — also known as WH40K or 40K — thought to be the most popular miniature wargame in the world. Battles are set in the distant future, leaving the technology department to hope the end of its long-running ERP saga comes before that date. ®
1d28d12072be0171: In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled. The big question now is how to enable predictive systems to act on their own conclusions without drifting from business intent. The frontier has moved from prediction to autonomous decision making, and the gap between leaders and laggards is widening accordingly.
“Enterprises are done with a backward-looking point of view; they want to be more forward-thinking,” says Vishal Gupta, partner at research firm Everest Group.

Intelligent analytics, powered by technologies like deep learning and generative AI, are making this possible. Real-time training allows AI to evolve continuously instead of waiting for quarterly refreshes. In addition, the data that newer predictive engines rely upon has expanded to encompass not just neat, numerical records but also messy, unstructured sources of insight-rich interactions. As a result, AI-powered analytics are moving enterprises from passive hindsight to pragmatic foresight.

AI takes predictive analytics—a broad discipline that includes predictive modeling, data prep, analysis workflows, interpretation of results, and decision-making applications—to new heights. “In many ways I think the word ‘analytics’ is giving way to AI,” says Gupta. “Everything is becoming AI.”
