77e834fa3020f5e0: PETALING JAYA: PAS mungkin bersedia menunggu lima hingga 10 tahun lagi sebelum secara serius menerajui kepimpinan tertinggi negara, kata bekas ketua penerangan Umno, Shahril Hamdan.
Baru-baru ini, PAS dan Umno berunding mengenai kerjasama menjelang PRN Melaka dengan PAS membayangkan keterbukaan bertanding di bawah logo Barisan Nasional (BN).
Minggu lalu, Mursyidul Am PAS Hashim Jasin, berkata pencapaian pakatan PAS-Umno pada PRN Melaka akan menjadi langkah penting memperluasnya ke PRU16, lapor Utusan Malaysia.

Bercakap dalam audio siar Keluar Sekejap, Shahril berkata PAS dan Umno dilihat bergerak berasaskan garis masa berbeza, di mana Umno lebih tertumpu untuk memenangi kuasa sekarang, manakala PAS kelihatan lebih bersedia untuk menunggu.

Beliau berkata, PAS mungkin bersedia menyertai kerajaan tanpa mendesak jawatan nombor satu secara serta-merta, sebaliknya menggunakan peluang berkenaan untuk memberi lebih pengalaman kepada pemimpinnya, selain membiasakan penjawat awam dan pengundi dengan parti mereka.
"Membiasakan lebih penting, membiasakan rakyat dengan wajah dan PAS berada dalam sesebuah kerajaan tak perlu ditakuti," katanya.

Shahril berkata, PAS – yang sedar ada sebahagian pengundi masih menganggapnya 'terlalu ekstrem', kurang kepakaran, dan kekurangan teknokrat berkeupayaan untuk mengendalikan urusan kementerian kanan – akan mengambil masa beberapa penggal untuk mengubah persepsi itu secara beransur-ansur.
"Dan transisi tu mungkin mengambil masa lima hingga 10 tahun lagi."

Katanya, beliau sudah pun melihat tanda peralihan sedemikian dalam perbualan dengan profesional Melayu, yang sebelum ini menganggap Umno sebagai parti Melayu yang lebih sederhana, namun kini melihat PAS sebagai pilihan yang boleh diterima di peti undi.

Rakan pengacara, Zaidel Baharuddin, bagaimanapun melontarkan persoalan mengapa PAS tidak menonjolkan seorang daripada pemimpinnya secara lebih dominan sebagai calon perdana menteri, dan mengapa Presiden Wawasan Hamzah Zainudin, dibenarkan kekal memegang peranan penting termasuk ketua pembangkang.
5ddf6f1248133930: PETALING JAYA: PAS may be prepared to wait another five to 10 years before making a serious push for the country’s top leadership, says former Umno information chief Shahril Hamdan.
PAS and Umno recently negotiated cooperation ahead of the Melaka state election, with the Islamic party indicating it is open to contesting under the Barisan Nasional logo.
PAS spiritual leader Hashim Jasin last week said achieving a PAS-Umno alliance in the Melaka polls would be a key step to expanding it to the 16th general election, Utusan Malaysia reported.
Speaking on the Keluar Sekejap podcast, Shahril said PAS and Umno appeared to be working on different timelines, with Umno more focussed on winning power now while PAS seemed more willing to wait.

He said PAS could be prepared to enter government without immediately demanding the top job, using the opportunity to give its leaders more experience and make civil servants and voters more familiar with the party.
“(PAS wants to) get the public used to seeing it in government,” he said.

Shahril said PAS – which was aware that some voters still viewed it as “too extreme”, lacking in expertise, and without enough technocrats capable of handling senior ministries – could spend several terms gradually changing that perception.
“I think they believe a transition is happening, and that transition may take another five to 10 years.”

He said he was already seeing signs of such a shift in conversations with Malay professionals, who had traditionally regarded Umno as the more moderate Malay party but were increasingly seeing PAS as a viable choice at the ballot box.

Co-host and Muda deputy president Zaidel Baharuddin, however, questioned why PAS had not pushed one of its leaders more prominently as a prime ministerial candidate, and why Wawasan president Hamzah Zainudin had been allowed to retain such a prominent role, including as opposition leader.
d696b4dd3044ecdd: KUALA LUMPUR: The Federal Government's Accounts Receivable (AR) fell by 1.1 per cent to RM102.032 billion in 2025 from RM103.158 billion the previous year, according to the Auditor General's Report 2/2026.

The report stated that the RM1.126 billion decrease was partly due to the write-off of revenue AR and loan interests amounting to RM1.207 billion, as well as RM603 million in guarantee fees no longer reported as AR.
Of the total, RM50.845 billion comprised Claimable Loans and Advances, while RM51.187 billion was Miscellaneous AR, down by 1.3 per cent and 0.9 per cent respectively, compared to 2024.
The report noted that non-compliance with the repayment schedule for Claimable Loans resulted in RM8.084 billion in arrears and RM578.32 million being written off.

The report also confirmed that total outstanding AR for utility relocation costs amounted to RM90.50 million. This amount includes RM30.46 million borne by the government, which should not have been recorded as outstanding AR.
The report recommended that the Federal Government strengthen its revenue collection mechanism through more strategic and effective measures.
This, it said, would help fund development expenditure more sustainably, reduce the fiscal deficit and decrease reliance on new borrowings.
It also suggested that the government take more proactive enforcement and monitoring actions to accelerate AR collection, reduce arrears and minimise the need for write-offs.
4b87fd8bcd73518e: KUALA LUMPUR: The public need to change the perception that universities are the only avenue for developing talent and determining the success of young people, said Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir.
He said knowledge and skills in technical fields also opened up career opportunities for young people, including those who were less academically inclined.

"Over the past two years, we have often told the people that universities are not the only place for them to pursue their studies, but we also have other skills institutions such as polytechnics and community colleges that offer skills certificates in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET).

"For years, society has viewed polytechnics as a second choice for those who cannot get into university, but now applications to enter polytechnics have reached 132 per cent compared with 60 to 70 per cent previously," he said.

He said this during the "Technology Driving Change: Is Malaysian Talent Ready?" dialogue session held in conjunction with the launch of the Future Skills Framework for the Communications Sector and the Strategic Talent Development Initiative at Angkasapuri today.
Zambry said teaching approaches at skills institutions were also being strengthened to meet the country's demand for technical workers, including the government's effort to produce 60,000 engineers.

He said technical and engineering fields did not necessarily depend solely on degree qualifications, but also required skilled workers who had undergone engineering-related training at skills institutions.

Students from the arts stream with an interest and potential in the field were also being given opportunities to pursue it through suitable intervention programmes, he said, adding that polytechnics had so far trained 447 students through engineering diploma programmes.

Meanwhile, Deputy Human Resources Minister Datuk Khairul Firdaus Akbar Khan said the skills mismatch issue needed attention, with nearly 37 per cent of skilled workers recorded as not working in the second quarter of this year, while the country's workforce stood at 16.8 million.

He said the situation was attributed, among other factors, to a lack of job opportunities, skills mismatches and less attractive salary offers in certain fields, making it necessary to strengthen the "future-proof talent" approach to ensure workers' skills were aligned earlier with future job requirements.

In efforts to strengthen workforce development, he said the Ministry of Human Resources had introduced the National Human Resources Policy 2026-2035, focusing on four aspects - more productive employment, career development, more meaningful incomes and appropriate protection.

However, Khairul Firdaus said the effectiveness of the policy needed to be supported by more balanced infrastructure development between states to ensure job opportunities and talent development were not concentrated only in the Klang Valley.

acb6d19da9686ede: NAGOYA, Oct 5 — The nine gold medals secured by the Malaysian contingent at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games matched the nation’s best-ever performance from Guangzhou 2010, more importantly, however, this achievement offers an opportunity to assess how the country’s sporting potential can be translated into even greater success in the future.
These successes came from karate, e-sports, sepak takraw, squash, and track cycling, enabling Malaysia to surpass the initial target of six gold medals set prior to the games.

Squash emerged as a key contributor with Ng Eain Yow and S. Sivasangari having already qualified for the Los Angeles Olympics (LA28) and defended their respective singles titles, while the men’s and women’s squads also dominated the team events.
The four gold medals from the sport cemented squash’s status as a primary medal prospect for the nation, while also reflecting the results of continuous athlete development efforts.
In sepak takraw, the men’s team regu gold held special significance, as Malaysia ended a 36-year wait to stand atop the podium in that event.
Track cycling ace Datuk Mohd Azizulhasni Awang leveraged his vast experience to win the men’s keirin, thereby ending Malaysia’s 16-year drought in the event.

Meanwhile, Taj Izrin Aiman Taj Madira made history as the country’s first e-sports representative to win an Asian Games gold medal triumphing in Gran Turismo 7 while Adeola Fay Robert and C. Shahmalarani contributed two gold medals in karate.

Collectively, these results demonstrate that Malaysia’s sporting strength is broadening and the nation is no longer solely reliant on traditional sports but is showcasing potential in new disciplines and involving athletes from different generations.
However, those nine gold medals should not overshadow certain issues that arose during the 16 days of competition in Aichi-Nagoya.

Several sports expected to contribute medals failed to meet their targets, while the men’s hockey squad missed the chance to secure gold and an automatic ticket to LA28 after losing to India in the final.

This situation demonstrates that a contingent’s strength cannot be measured solely by medal count, rather, it depends on the ability of each sport to capitalise on opportunities when facing top-level competition.

Therefore, the achievements in Aichi-Nagoya should serve as a basis for re-evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of each sport, including aspects such as talent development, coaching, competition preparation, and sports science and medical support.

National Sports Council (NSC) director-general Jefri Ngadirin described the achievement as a positive indicator that the country’s high-performance sports development programme is on the right track, though he cautioned that this success is not the final destination.

In addition to the nine gold medals, the national contingent brought home seven silver and 16 bronze medals, demonstrating that Malaysia retains a solid foundation to remain competitive at the Asian level.

However, an even greater challenge lies ahead as Malaysia prepares to host the 2027 SEA Games, before attention shifts to LA28, the nation’s primary target in the quest to realise the dream of winning its first Olympic gold medal.
Aichi-Nagoya ultimately saw Malaysia secure nine gold medals, matching the best record set at Guangzhou 2010.
However, the true value of this achievement should not be measured solely by that figure.

Instead, these nine gold medals should serve as a starting point to identify what worked well, address remaining weaknesses, and build continuity, ensuring that the success in Aichi-Nagoya does not merely repeat history, but acts as a springboard for even greater achievements on the international stage. — Bernama
b57368bb9d2a0ad6: STOCKHOLM, Oct 5 — Since 1901, the Nobel Prizes have been awarded to individuals and organisations for work leading to great advances for humanity, in line with the wishes of the prizes’ founder, inventor Alfred Nobel.
The 2026 winners will be announced between October 5 and 12, starting with the Nobel Prize in Medicine on Monday from 11:30 am (0930 GMT).
Here are five things to know about the prizes and their founder.
In detention
Since 1901, five Nobel Peace Prize laureates have been prevented from attending the awards ceremony in Oslo.
In 1936, German journalist and pacifist Carl von Ossietzky was detained in a Nazi concentration camp.

Myanmar opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi was under house arrest when she won the prize in 1991. Given permission by the junta to travel, she declined for fear of potentially not being able to return to her country.
In 2010, Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo was in prison. His chair remained empty, where the prize was placed.
In 2022, Belarusian human rights campaigner Ales Bialiatski was in jail. He was represented by his wife Natalia Pinchuk.
In 2023, Iranian activist Narges Mohammadi was held in Iran’s Evin prison when the prize was awarded.
Young and old
In 2014, 17-year-old Pakistani human rights activist Malala Yousafzai became the youngest winner of a Nobel Prize.
Another unusually young laureate was Australia’s Lawrence Bragg, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics jointly with his father in 1915 when he was 25, for work carried out at the age of 21.
Iraqi activist Nadia Murad was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 25 in 2018 for her efforts on behalf of the Yazidi minority.

In contrast, American John Goodenough was the oldest to become a Nobel laureate. He won the Prize in Chemistry in 2019 at the age of 97 for his work on the lithium-ion batteries that power smartphones and electric cars.
The year before, his compatriot Arthur Ashkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics at the age of 96.
Posthumous awards
Since 1974, the statutes of the Nobel Foundation stipulate that the prize may not be given posthumously.
But the prize may still be awarded if the recipient dies between the time of the announcement in October and the formal prize ceremony in December.
Before the change, only two people had won a Nobel Prize posthumously.
One was Dag Hammarskjold, the Swedish secretary-general of the United Nations, who died in a plane crash in 1961 but was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize later the same year.
And in 1931, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded posthumously to another Swede, poet Erik Axel Karlfeldt.
In 2011, the committee for the Nobel Prize in Medicine selected Ralph Steinman of Canada, unaware that he had passed away just three days before the announcement.
The foundation nevertheless gave him the award.
Women laureates
Only 68 of the 633 Nobel prizes awarded since 1901 have been given to women, representing about 10 percent, though the share has been steadily increasing since the early 2020s.

The science fields have the lowest representation of women laureates. The various committees that award the prizes have repeatedly refused to introduce quotas, instead encouraging nominations of women scientists.

Only five women have won a Nobel physics prize out of a total of 230 laureates in the discipline, three out of 99 economics laureates, eight out of 200 chemistry laureates, and 14 out of 232 medicine laureates.
Marie Curie was the first woman laureate in 1903 and she is to this day the only woman to have received two Nobel prizes, first for physics in 1903 and then in 1911 in chemistry.
Nobel the poet
Nobel went down in history as the inventor of dynamite but he also loved English poetry and was an admirer of Percy Bysshe Shelley and Byron.
He wrote poetry himself his entire life, sometimes in his native Swedish but mostly in English.
In a letter to a friend, he wrote: “I have not the slightest pretension to call my verses poetry; I write now and then for no other purpose than to relieve depression, or to improve my English.”
In 1862, at the age of 29 and questioning his literary talent, he sent a letter in French to a young woman that said: “Physics is my field, not writing.”

In 1896, the year of his death, he wrote a scandalous tragedy in four acts titled “Nemesis”, inspired by Shelley’s play “The Cenci” about a woman in 16th-century Rome who murders her incestuous father. — AFP

bb8f8722e2003b45: PETALING JAYA: The authorities should have anticipated the transport problems that left tens of thousands of F1 fans stranded during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit, says former Umno information chief Shahril Hamdan.

a93422f1d0552308: RIYADH: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces seized key positions on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Monday, military and government sources said, as they fought to reverse last month's advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and drive them from the vital waterway.

The government forces have taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks Bab el-Mandeb, and are asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition, three military sources and one government source told Reuters.
Houthi-aligned media had earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area.

Fighting has raged along several frontlines in Yemen for weeks after a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.

With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Hormuz Strait, the fighting in Yemen has threatened another major oil export route, pushing up global prices and raising new risks in a region already aflame.

The internationally recognised Yemeni government announced on Sunday the launch of its offensive to recapture territory, with President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia."
Saudi Arabia backs offensive to retake territory

Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory.

While the war has raged on several frontlines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around the city of Taiz, where the Houthis are trying to surround government forces.

A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying that the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council.

The mountainous district sits close to the main road running from Taiz to Aden, the last route that government forces have had into the city, which has been on the frontlines since early in the civil war.

Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the Iran-backed group.

The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate, with most frontlines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022 that held until this summer.
dff0248f30acbc3b: PARIS: A 15-year-old student lost a hand on Monday picking up a police grenade as part of nationwide protests over classroom conditions that have disrupted lessons at hundreds of schools since last week.
Some students returned to classrooms, but others maintained actions outside their schools, ahead of a day of larger demonstrations expected on Tuesday.

Authorities said the teenager was injured in the northern town of Lens. A police union source said he appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police and that it exploded in his hand.

Since late September, students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of schools, complaining of teacher absences, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings ill-adapted to rising temperatures, among other grievances.
The unrest erupted just months to go before 2027 elections that will determine the successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing hard-left activists of having hijacked the protest movement.
The French Human Rights League (LDH) on Monday accused security forces of using disproportionate methods against protesters, many of whom are legally minors.
"We can see that in the instructions given to the police, there is no directive to show restraint, even though they are dealing with children," LDH president Nathalie Tehio said.
Dustbins ablaze
More than 400 out of France's 3,700 high schools, known as lycees, were partially or totally closed on Monday morning, the education ministry said.
A third of the 468 lycees for teenagers aged 15 to 17 were expected to be closed in the Paris region, authorities said.
In central Paris, dozens of teenage students demonstrated outside a school while passing cars honked their horns. Some classmates made their way inside to attend lessons.
"We're missing our lessons to give you one," read one cardboard sign outside the Turgot high school, located in Paris's 3rd arrondissement.
In Bordeaux, in the southwest, some students returned to the classroom while others continued to demonstrate in the presence of riot police.

Some protesters outside the Gustave Eiffel high school set off fireworks in the direction of the police, who responded sporadiacally with tear gas, but overall the situation remained calm, AFP reporters said.
In the northern city of Lille, masked protesters destroyed bus shelters and set fire to dustbins, as police fired tear gas towards demonstrators.
The movement started on Sept 17 at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, in support of teachers striking over a lack of staff and resources.

It gained momentum and spread across France, at times spiralling into vandalism, including the destruction of bus shelters, the burning of school entrances and clashes between protesters and security forces.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools had been burned or ransacked, according to the education minister.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested.
Protesters have also accused the police of using excessive force, and internal investigations have been opened into at least three instances of alleged police brutality.
'Parental responsibility'
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu set out a timetable on Sunday urging local authorities to prioritise filling gaps left by long-term teacher absences and unfilled posts.
He called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country's often-dilapidated school buildings.
The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of drawing on public funds.
Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon defended the bill.

"When you have 14-, 15-, and 16-year-olds who, at 9 am, are burning bus shelters or – perhaps even more seriously – the high school where they study, that raises the question of parental responsibility," she told the Europe1/CNews broadcaster.
Lecornu has said the draft law could allow compensation payments to be recovered from family allowances and housing benefits while preserving a minimum income threshold.
The head of the main CGT labour union, Sophie Binet, slammed what she called a "populist announcement", which she said would "end up targeting the most vulnerable families".

5319f20344ff1662: Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques “So, where did you go to school?” On the face of it, it doesn’t seem like a loaded question. I was mostly bemused when I first started university 20 years ago and found myself being asked it repeatedly by other students. Why were they so interested? Surely no one would have heard of the north Wales comprehensive I had attended? When they countered my baffled reaction with “Charterhouse” or “Marlborough”, how was I supposed to respond? When one student said, of another, “He went to Winchester, you know”, I stared blankly at him, not understanding why he was telling me about someone else’s day trip to a city in Hampshire (“Oh, did he have a nice time?”). It was strange, new territory. Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports of classism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said. The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded. Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

7bb178406108f4bc: STOCKHOLM, Oct 5 — The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics.
Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviours like learning, fear, addiction and movement.
The trio were honoured “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells”, the Nobel Assembly said.
Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in a brain.
They have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

In clinical medicine, the method is being used in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment, and may one day lead to treatments for disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.

“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.
The secretary general of the assembly, Thomas Perlmann, told reporters he was able to reach the three laureates by phone to break the news.
“That was great to talk to them. I first called Deisseroth, he was very tired when he answered. He was definitely asleep, but he woke up,” he said.
Illumination
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel were examining why a single-celled alga was able to swim toward a light source.
They discovered an algal protein with unique properties, called channelrhodopsin, found on the surface of the cell.
When illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein.
Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that any cell they put the protein in became light sensitive.
Deisseroth then introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats.
By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal.
He published his breakthrough in 2005, and two years later, made the light-controlled switch for nerve cells work in the brains of living mice.
In 2021, Deisseroth and Hegemann won the Lasker Prize for their work in the field, often considered a precursor to the Nobel.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin.
Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg.
The Nobel prize for physics will be announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.
Some pundits have suggested that for literature, the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Central or Latin America.
Argentine author Samanta Schweblin, 48, could be one such pick, literary critic Lina Kalmteg told AFP.
All eyes on peace
Perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize — the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo.
This year, some experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, stirred controversy.

Among possible laureates this year are a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.

Others include Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) after the deadliest year on record for the profession in 2025.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.

This year’s laureates will receive their prizes — a diploma, a gold medal and a US$1.2-million (RM4.9 million) cheque — on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of the prize’s creator, scientist Alfred Nobel. — AFP
6da67098251352d7: The vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realities JD Vance has parachuted into the midterm election campaign on a rescue mission in a new guise: a risk management consultant. Speaking in the flat language of the expert hired to identify threats, weaknesses and losses affecting a business’s reputation, he has presented his executive summary for limiting vulnerabilities and a scenario for averting disaster. “There’s a lot of good that’s been done, but there’s a lot of work left to do,” he informed his clients on 15 September about the words to use. “Give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years.” He turned the focus to harm reduction rather than total agreement and then shifted the equation to a negative binary choice. “Even if you don’t agree with us on every issue, the other party is consumed by craziness.” Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast Continue reading...
81b8c09448309bbb: TAIZ, Oct 5 — Yemen’s military backed by Saudi jets attacked Houthi targets on Monday as they launched an ambitious campaign to recapture all territory from the Iran-backed group after its lightning gains during the Middle East war.
The military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes, while 100 warplanes attacked at dawn, according to the Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen’s government.
Yemen’s government announced the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory — much of it held for more than a decade — on Sunday.
Last month the Houthis seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping.

As the offensive began, a source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack on Sunday had again halted pumping in the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz.
The long-running conflict in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries and neighbour of Saudi Arabia, has flared anew months into the Middle East war that has sent crude prices soaring.

Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles are “scarily thin” owing to the US-Iran war, days after G7 nations agreed to release more of their inventories to ease supply concerns.
“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin.”
The Houthis have targeted Saudi oil infrastructure and tankers in the Red Sea since a ceasefire in Yemen’s civil war unravelled in July.
The group has accused the Saudi-led coalition of carrying out hundreds of strikes.
‘Stay and die’

A day after the new offensive was declared, Yemen’s military spokesman announced over 1,000 “strikes against artillery and rocket launcher positions, defensive fortifications, approach and reinforcement routes, supply lines and logistics assets, combat reinforcements”.

Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said 100 jets flew at daybreak as part of “Operation ‘Dawn of Yemen’“. They provided “round-the-clock air support for the Yemeni armed forces on the ground”, he wrote on X.
The strikes have yet to blunt ongoing Houthi advances on the ground.
On Sunday, the group effectively encircled the key city of Taiz after cutting the main supply route linking the city to the interim government capital of Aden.
However, Taiz residents remained defiant, vowing to stay and defend their city.
“We cannot leave the city. It is impossible for us to leave. We will stay and die inside this city,” Fahmi Ahmed Ghaleb told AFP.
“Throughout the earlier clashes with the Houthis, we also stayed inside the city.”
Humanitarian crisis
Taiz city remains under the control of government forces but has long been encircled from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s war.

The Houthis’ surrounding of Taiz “is a significant development, but I think it is still too early to say that we are witnessing a decisive turning point”, Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told AFP.
While the war in Yemen predates the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become the most active front in the wider conflict in recent weeks.
The Houthis launched a rapid offensive around the Red Sea coast in September that killed hundreds of combatants on both sides and, according to UN figures, displaced more than 145,000 people.
The Houthis took control of Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing out the internationally recognised government. They hold much of Yemen, including its most populous areas.

The Saudi-led international military coalition intervened in March 2015. The ensuing civil war caused hundreds of thousands of deaths and a spiralling humanitarian crisis that left a majority of the population relying on aid. — AFP
d7a9d8985da09831: JAKARTA, Oct 5 — Malaysia secured third place in the Fifa Asean Cup 2026 after edging Vietnam 1-0 in their third-place playoff at Gelora Bung Karno (GBK) Stadium here, today.
Substitute Fergus Tierney emerged the hero for Harimau Malaya, scoring the only goal in the 62nd minute to hand interim head coach Tan Cheng Hoe’s side a winning finish to their campaign.

Cheng Hoe made three changes to his starting line-up, resting defensive mainstay Brad Tapp and sensational winger Arif Aiman Mohd Hanapi, while captain Dion Cools was unavailable after leaving the national camp due to urgent family matters.

Vietnam looked the more threatening side in the opening half, repeatedly probing Malaysia’s defence with attacking moves and high crosses that kept the backline and goalkeeper Ahmad Syihan Hazmi busy.

Malaysia, however, came closest to breaking the deadlock in the 39th minute when naturalised striker Bergson da Silva produced a skilful dribbling manoeuvre to beat a Vietnam defender, but his effort was saved by goalkeeper Patrik Le Giang.
Vietnam under head coach Kim Sang-sik responded four minutes later through Nguyen Hai Long, whose close-range free-kick was comfortably gathered by Ahmad Syihan.
In first-half stoppage time, Ngo Dang Khoa tried his luck from outside the penalty area but his effort drifted narrowly wide of Ahmad Syihan’s right post.
Vietnam continued to threaten after the restart, with Williams Minh Hoang firing a low effort narrowly wide of the left post in the 57th minute.
Malaysia responded two minutes later when Bergson beat the offside trap, but his powerful strike went wide of the right post.
However, Tierney made an immediate impact after replacing Bergson, receiving Manuel Hidalgo’s pass before turning sharply and unleashing a powerful shot past Le Giang to give Malaysia the lead.

Ahmad Syihan and the defence then worked tirelessly to protect their lead, including denying Le Pham Thanh Long’s effort in the closing stages to complete the tournament without conceding a single goal.

The victory allowed Malaysia to end the tournament on a positive note after narrowly missing out on a place in the final on goals scored, despite finishing level with hosts Indonesia on points and goal difference in Division 1 Group A.

The victory also ended Malaysia’s more than a decade-long winless run against Vietnam, with their last victory over the regional rivals coming in the second leg of the 2014 AFF Cup semi-finals. — Bernama
19d891c24d0ba926: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Safety issues in schools should not be concealed to protect reputations, as this may prevent authorities from taking action, said Inspector-General of Police Tan Sri Mohd Khalid Ismail.
He said cooperation between the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) and schools should be strengthened to ensure all incidents are reported for further action.

“Sometimes there are actions by certain parties attempting to hide issues to protect their reputation. But I believe if we enhance and strengthen this relationship, it can help resolve the problems,” he told a press conference after the launch of the PDRM Negotiator Handbook at the Bukit Aman Senior Officers' Mess here today.

Mohd Khalid said school safety is a shared responsibility requiring cooperation among PDRM, schools, the Ministry of Education, and parents. School liaison officers also regularly visit and coordinate with school authorities on safety issues.

He added that PDRM holds regular discussions with schools and parent-teacher associations on safety measures, including proposals to install closed-circuit television (CCTV). The Crime Prevention and Community Safety Department (JPJKK) has also increased patrols at schools and hostels.
On the death of a 16-year-old student at a school in Yong Peng, Johor, he said some details remain unconfirmed and the department will conduct a thorough investigation before making any conclusions.
Meanwhile, Mohd Khalid said PDRM has strengthened its Negotiator Cell, which was set up two years ago, by introducing a handbook for officers to use during crisis negotiations.

He said the cell, under the Internal Security and Public Order Department (KDNKA), has about 40 officers from various departments. The officers are selected based on their experience and can be deployed if a crisis requires negotiation expertise.
"If a crisis such as a kidnapping occurs, requiring advice, views, or negotiation between relevant parties, we will call upon the officers concerned to carry out the negotiation," he said.
He said the Negotiator Cell also works with other PDRM divisions as needed. The unit has also given lectures and shared experience in crisis management with the Royal Brunei Police Force.

Bukit Aman KDNKA deputy director (Crisis and Disaster) and Negotiator Cell commandant Datuk M.V Srikumar Nair said no standard response time is set for each case, as the duration depends on the circumstances and uniqueness of an incident.
"Every case is unique. Some information is received quickly, while other cases take time. Therefore, there is no standard response time," he said. — Bernama
b43000d93607564d: Ubuntu 26.10, “Stonking Stingray,” has entered beta testing, slightly later than planned – it is in fact scheduled to be released on October 15. While many people will stay with the LTS version, there’s some interesting stuff in there. There are already some release notes, but like the OS itself, they aren’t final yet, and there are still some gaps. Canonical does note that the "oxidization" process – exchanging core Unix tools written in C with new Rust replacements – goes further in this edition: now, the stock OpenPGP encryption support is via the Rust-based Sequoia-PGP. Perhaps one of the most daringly different new features is Canonical’s promised LLM-powered Myna speech-to-text tool. This isn’t installed by default, but you can add it, and a choice of speech-recognition models. We found various sets of instructions, including the unofficial “Ubuntu Handbook”. Our geriatric testbed was a little old for this, though, and we couldn't try it. A couple of weeks ago we took at look at the beta of what will become Fedora 45. Both Ubuntu 26.10 and the default workstation edition of Fedora will use GNOME 51, but since the Fedora beta, the final release of the latest GNOME is here: GNOME 51 “A Coruña”. The version in the Ubuntu beta isn’t working completely smoothly. We saw a persistent error about missing themes, and although the OS offered to install whatever was missing automatically, this failed. Since it doesn’t actually say what is missing, we can’t install it ourselves. The problem is only cosmetic: just some missing icons in applications, very similar to what we saw in Alpine Linux 3.16 four years ago. Sadly, problems around GNOME themes are a long standing issue. As we reported earlier this year, the Linux Mint developers are still struggling with them. The occasional missing icon aside, though, Stonking works pretty well. We tried both in a Virtualbox VM and on bare metal on our old testbed Thinkpad W520, and it ran well in both. The new installation program that arrived with the 2024 LTS version works fine, and now makes it much clearer which control is currently selected with an orange highlight. We do wish the window was resizable, though. The testbed machine has two SATA drives and we had to do a lot of scrolling to choose the right partitions. It also failed to use our dedicated swap partition, although we selected it during installation. Although GNOME 51 removed their support for old Nvidia devices in this development cycle, it still picked up and used the machine’s Nvidia-controlled Displayport output. It didn’t work perfectly: GNOME couldn’t report on the model or properties of our Quadro 1000 GPU, or the CPU-integrated Intel one for that matter, but at least the second screen worked. More surprisingly, it even worked in the Fallback session, even though that uses the Metacity X11 window manager – and while logged into to a Fallback session, it could identify both GPUs. GNOME 51 isn’t a very feature-heavy release, but the Settings app has some useful additions, such as the ability to automatically disable the trackpad when an external mouse is connected. In our testing, it picked up and let us configure mouse, trackpad, and trackpoint, each in a separate tab. GNOME 51 no longer supports Wi-Fi networks with the old WEP encryption system, though. Modern Linux continues to move away from being an OS for old and low-end hardware. If the machine is online during installation, the installer fetches any package updates as it works, so the first update post-install is much quicker. However, this doesn’t apply to Snap packages: the .deb package phase of our first update was very fast, but we got various new snaps. One detail we haven’t noticed before is that while a snap application is updating, its dock icon temporarily gets a progress bar to tell you it’s being updated. We did a full install with all the optional extras, so this applied to Thunderbird as well as Firefox. A full installation took a fairly hefty 13 GB of disk space, although to be fair, that included 4GB of swap space – so in real money, it’s about 9 GB, which isn’t too bad for 2026. According to the htop command, it idles at about 1.2 B RAM, which is quite high, but then GNOME is no lightweight. Linux kernel 7.3 is still in development, but at the time of writing it’s up to RC5, and our testing ran without a hitch. The final version may be out before “Stonking” is completed, but if not, users will get it very soon afterwards. We also gave the Kubuntu desktop a very brief try. In this release, it uses Plasma 6.7.5, and ran well – it was fast, smooth, and happily drove both screens of our testbed machine; helpfully, on our first login, it asked where the second display was relative to the first. If you want modern Wayland niceties such as different dots-per-inch settings on different screens, but you also want a traditional Windows-style layout, KDE is currently the way to go. Plasma 6.8 is scheduled for later this month, and totally drops X11 support. It’s likely to be the desktop in Kubuntu 27.04, making it Wayland-only – so 26.10 is probably the last ever version of Kubuntu in which displaying your desktop thanks to X.org is a supported option. We installed X11 support, which is just one command: sudo apt install -y plasma-session-x11 This brings in multiple extra dependencies, which is why we specified the -y switch, but it took just seconds. We logged out, logged back again choosing “Plasma (X11)”, and… Everything looked absolutely identical. Which is how it should be, of course. Both screens were working normally, thanks to the Nouveau FOSS NVIDIA driver. The only visible differences are the classic “wobbly window” effect when moving windows around, and that the title-bar context menu regains the option to “shade” a window: roll it up, leaving only the title bar visible. You can’t do this in a Wayland environment. Under Wayland, htop reports about 1.2 GB in use; under X.org, about 1.3 GB. The resurrected Oxygen theme from KDE 4 is built in, if you want a bit more visual bling, but we preferred the flatter grayer look of the default Breeze theme. The only freeze that we saw in all our testing of the Stonking beta was after logging out of a Plasma (Wayland) session and trying to log back in using Plasma (X11). To be fair, we suspect most people wouldn’t chop-and-change this much. Ubuntu Stonking is shaping up well. Aside from the small theme-related glitches, GNOME worked fine, and KDE didn’t even have those minor issues. The equivalent beta versions of all the official flavors are also available, including both Ubuntu Unity 26.10 and Ubuntu MATE. Despite a hundred other distros, Ubuntu remains the go-to desktop Linux for most people. While Canonical is getting slightly more experimental with interim releases again, this is a mature product now and they’re a pretty safe bet. ®
2c8ea11be98cbba1: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — The ringgit closed higher against most Asean currencies but eased against the US dollar on Monday, amid renewed concerns over France’s public finances following a sharp sell-off in its bond market last week.
At 6pm, the ringgit eased to 4.0845/0890 against the greenback from Friday’s close of 4.0820/0870.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd Chief Economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the US Dollar Index (DXY) gained further momentum as risk-off sentiment prevailed amid concerns over public finances and political upheaval in European economies.
“The euro fell to a 17-month low on Monday following news of a snap election in Spain.
“Hence, the ringgit remained in a tight range against the US dollar thus far,” he told Bernama.
The ringgit traded mixed against a basket of major currencies.

The local note rose against the euro to 4.5775/5825 from 4.5927/5983 at Friday’s close and gained against the Japanese yen to 2.5858/5886 from 2.5906/5941. However, it depreciated against the British pound to 5.4022/4081 from 5.3927/3993.
Meanwhile, the ringgit traded mostly higher against Asean currencies.

872ba13537162fc5: The mechanical keyboard isn't always so mechanical anymore.

Over the past six years, keyboards with optical, Hall-effect, and other "contactless" switches have become increasingly common, often going for higher prices than traditional mechanical keyboards, which already command a premium over basic membrane boards. In return, they promise some theoretical advantages, particularly for gamers. In daily use, though, the differences can be pretty subtle.

So what exactly are you paying for? In this guide, we break down how the newest switches work, why contactless designs are becoming more popular, and where their advantages—and disadvantages—really matter.
f2e253646db7f667: BATU PAHAT, Oct 5 — The Johor state government is ready to review and assist with basic infrastructure needs in schools across the state to strengthen security measures, says Johor Menteri Besar Datuk Onn Hafiz Ghazi.
He said this is to prevent a recurrence of the incident that led to the death of 16-year-old Form Four student Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal at a secondary school in Yong Peng, near here.

Onn Hafiz expressed full support for any initiative implemented by the Education Ministry (MOE), particularly the installation of closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras in strategic areas within school premises.

"We have received a report on the incident and will look into every angle and opportunity to ensure student safety is better guaranteed," he said, adding that he would liaise with the ministry regarding student safety issues.

Speaking to reporters after visiting the victim's family in Kampung Parit Selamat today, he expressed deep sorrow on behalf of the state government, while urging the public to give police space to conduct a thorough investigation and refrain from speculation.

Meanwhile, State Education and Information Committee chairman Dr Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali said discussions would be held soon between the Johor State Education Department (JPNJ) and the Batu Pahat District Education Office (PPD).
He said the meeting would re-examine safety standard operating procedures (SOPs) in detail to address any existing weaknesses or shortcomings.
"This is not a matter to be taken lightly as it involves the loss of a life," he said.
On Saturday (Oct 3), Irene Sofiya was found unconscious and bleeding in the school hall at about 5.50 pm.
Johor Police chief Datuk Ab Rahaman Arsad said the victim sustained injuries to her head and body and was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police subsequently detained a 16-year-old boy in Yong Peng at about 7 pm the same day. He was later remanded in custody for six days until Oct 9 to assist in investigations under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder. — Bernama
7f17f06fe08092b4: TOKYO, Oct 5 — Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz advanced to the final of the Japan Open on Monday after securing a hard-fought 5-7, 6-3, 6-1 victory over fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar in Tokyo.
The world number three clinched the win despite struggling with mistakes, particularly near the end of the first set, while his 49th-ranked opponent put up a brave fight.

Alcaraz unleashed a barrage of big serves and aggressive returns to keep Munar off-balance and running along the baseline, occasionally mixing in delicate drop shots that wowed the packed crowd at the Ariake Colosseum.
Munar maintained his composure to stay competitive especially late in the opening set, as Alcaraz hit shots wide and long and racked up four double-faults in that set alone.
Nevertheless, Alcaraz kept pressure on his opponent, showering him with precise forehands, fast volleys and drop shots, breaking Munar’s serve in the first, third and ninth games of the second set.
Alcaraz dominated the final set, wrapping up the match in two hours and 31 minutes.
In the final, Alcaraz will face either Jiri Lehecka of Czechia or Valentin Vacherot from Monaco, who are set to square off in the other semi-final later Monday. — AFP
eb11b6b04f311585: BEIJING, Oct 5 — Former world number one Iga Swiatek staged a comeback to advance to the last 16 at the China Open on Monday, while home hope Zheng Qinwen survived another three-set test in Beijing.
Swiatek overcame frustration to cling on as her opponent served for the set, dominating a must-win tie-break to beat Croatia’s Donna Vekic 4-6, 7-6 (7/0), 6-2.
“I was just angry, wanted to change something, because clearly it wasn’t working,” the 25-year-old from Poland said on court.
“Sometimes if you care a bit less because you’re... probably going to lose, it also helps you a bit,” she later told reporters.
She will face American teenager Iva Jovic for a spot in the quarter-finals.
China’s Zheng was tested by Marie Bouzkova, enduring her third three-setter of the tournament to beat the Czech player 7-6 (7/3), 4-6, 7-5.
Zheng voiced frustration in each set at movement outside the court, including as she tried to salvage the second set on Bouzkova’s serve.
But she pulled out some of her most accurate tennis to clinch the last two games and win the match when 27th-ranked Bouzkova fired long.
“I gave everything,” said Zheng, who had already spent more than five hours on court in the first two rounds.
“Truthfully speaking, I felt a lot of pressure today,” the 23-year-old told her home crowd, thanking fans for their support but commenting on distractions during play.
“Sometimes I’m a bit screaming in Chinese, because I really see you guys are moving, but next match I hope I will be better on this,” she said.
Zheng, the current world number 54, next plays 118th-ranked Alina Charaeva, who sent out top seed Elena Rybakina in the second round.
Coco Gauff, the highest-ranked player left in the women’s draw, was due to play Chinese 16-year-old Sun Xinran later on Monday.
Alex de Minaur was scheduled to play Hubert Hurkacz for the first spot in the men’s final before a blockbuster clash between former world number ones Novak Djokovic and Daniil Medvedev.
Djokovic, 39, beat top seed Alexander Zverev in a three-set thriller on Sunday, extending his unbeaten streak in Beijing to 32 matches. — AFP
e930a456bdb0f1fc: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Good governance practices must continue to be upheld, while any form of unauthorised land encroachment must not be taken lightly as it could affect national planning and the interests of the people, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.

He said enforcement must therefore continue to be strengthened, while any related issues raised by stakeholders, including non-governmental organisations (NGOs), should be addressed promptly to ensure accurate and transparent information is communicated comprehensively and effectively.
In a Facebook post today, Anwar said he stressed these points while chairing the 83rd National Land Council meeting.
“As we confront the effects of climate change, land governance can no longer focus solely on economic returns or physical development.
“Land management must be carried out prudently and systematically to minimise risks to environmental sustainability,” he said.
Anwar said the Madani Government would continue to ensure that land management initiatives were carried out responsibly for the benefit of the people. — Bernama
0b3a307f64bcd35c: GENEVA, Oct 5 — Switzerland looks on course Monday to hold a referendum on a trade deal with Malaysia, with opponents believing the agreement endangers tropical rainforests and lacks proper safeguards against forced labour.
Campaigners handed in 85,000 signatures at the parliament buildings in the Swiss capital Bern on Monday, public broadcaster RTS said.

To trigger a referendum under Switzerland’s direct democracy system, 50,000 valid signatures must be collected within 100 days of publication of a new law. The Swiss parliament completed its approval of the trade deal in June.
The authorities will now have to verify the signatures.
If approved, the referendum would likely go ahead in the first half of 2027.
The free trade agreement is between Malaysia and the European Free Trade Association that brings together Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, all countries outside the European Union.
The EFTA-Malaysia Economic Partnership Agreement was signed at EFTA’s ministerial meeting in Tromso, Norway, in June 2025.
The agreement comes into effect once the domestic ratification processes in the contracting states have been completed, Switzerland said when the deal was signed.

“For Malaysian palm oil, Switzerland has agreed to a market-compatible and quota-based reduction in tariffs so as not to adversely affect domestic production of vegetable oils,” authorities said at the time.

“The agreement also includes a comprehensive section on environmental protection and labour rights. Among other things, it contains specific provisions to ensure that palm oil traded under the agreement is produced sustainably.”
In Switzerland, palm oil is primarily used in processed foods, cosmetics and cleaning products.
The Alliance Against Tropical Deforestation umbrella organisation led the collection of signatures against the deal.
The agreement “plans to lower tariffs on 12,500 tonnes of palm oil, without effective measures against rainforest deforestation and forced labour”, the alliance says.

“In doing so, Switzerland is helping to accelerate the destruction of a rainforest in Malaysia that is already critically threatened, while jeopardising the rights of plantation workers and indigenous communities.
“Furthermore, this agreement risks restricting the right of farming families to freely save and exchange their seeds,” it claims.

According to EFTA figures, Switzerland exported €890 million (RM4.08 billion) of goods to Malaysia in 2025, led by pharmaceutical products, (€255 million) and machinery and mechanical appliances (€191 million).
Imports from Malaysia to Switzerland were worth €622 million, led by electrical machinery (€244 millon) and machinery and mechanical appliances (€109 million). — AFP
ec9695a53f16ed28: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Bursa Malaysia closed slightly higher today, in line with upbeat regional markets, as improved risk appetite was supported by softer US labour data, that reduced expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening and eased pressure on bond yields.
At 5pm, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 0.88 of-a-point to 1,631.75 from last Friday’s close of 1,630.87.
The benchmark index, which opened 2.55 points higher at 1,633.42, moved between 1,630.95 and 1,640.46 throughout the trading session.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said technology shares were among the main beneficiaries.

Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index edged up 0.45 of a point to 178.97, the Financial Services Index garnered 99.63 points to 19,140.14, while the Energy Index shaved off 3.09 points to 829.94, and the Plantation Index tumbled 125.52 points to 8,931.03.
The Main Market volume expanded to 3.13 billion units worth RM2.41 billion from 2.67 billion units worth RM2.34 billion last Friday.
Warrants turnover rose to 1.04 billion units worth RM208.20 million from 973.40 million units worth RM160.21 million previously.
The ACE Market volume climbed to 611.02 million units valued at RM267.66 million from 593.05 million units valued at RM205.21 million on Friday.

Meanwhile, consumer products and services counters accounted for 248.10 million shares traded on the Main Market, industrial products and services (439.37 million), construction (183.56 million), technology (1.76 billion), financial services (49.02 million), property (106.95 million), plantation (22.08 million), real estate investment trusts (10.76 million), closed-end fund (152,900), energy (106.66 million), healthcare (103.20 million), telecommunications and media (22.11 million), transportation and logistics (40.92 million), utilities (38.48 million), and business trusts (162,200). — Bernama
9c29b4d1a250219c: The first year of Windows 10 Extended Security Updates is coming to an end, and Windows 11's market share has ticked up as enterprises weigh up the cost of keeping Windows 10 running a little longer. Windows 11's market share has risen above 70 percent to 71.5 percent, while Windows 10's has dropped to 27.77 percent, according to statistics wrangler Statcounter. Microsoft does not provide official statistics on Windows 11 and 10 usage, so Statcounter's figures should be treated as estimates. They are derived from Statcounter's tracking code, which is installed on over 1 million sites globally. The shares have remained relatively static since a surge in Windows 11 adoption at the end of last year, likely driven by the upgrade wave after Windows 10 dropped out of support on Oct 14, 2025. The Extended Security Updates (ESU) program allowed holdouts to stick with Windows 10, but the first year of that program is coming to an end, and kind old Microsoft will be hiking the prices for year two, at least as far as commercial customers are concerned. ESU licenses cost $61 per device for the first year for commercial users. Microsoft stated that the price would double every consecutive year for a maximum of three years, meaning that a renewal for year two will come in at $122. There are ways around the charge, of course. As well as consumers who can stay with Windows 10 and receive free security updates in return for redeeming Microsoft Rewards Points or using Windows Backup to sync their settings to the cloud, Windows 365 users are also exempt. It's also worth noting that European Economic Area (EEA) consumers receive no-strings-attached security updates. However, enterprises that need Windows 10 security updates must pay for them, as they did with other Microsoft products the software biz moved on from despite large user bases. The rising cost may be prompting some to reassess their estates. This month's uptick, while far short of last year's surge, could signal a sizeable ripple as the economics of keeping Windows 10 devices supported begin to favor Windows 11. Enterprises have plenty of reasons to keep Windows 10 devices: that one weird bit of hardware that won't work with anything else, or a simple case of a refresh cycle not fitting in with Microsoft's demand that old kit be junked to allow new software to run. Esben Dochy, a principal technology evangelist at Lansweeper, told The Register that its data indicated enterprises had been very active in moving off Windows 10 during the first year of ESU, with what is left being much "stickier." He reckoned there would be a "small bump" around the renewal date, and said, "The ESU price doubles for the second year, and that makes the business case for replacing the 'we'll get to it' machines a lot easier," but noted "it's likely that the steep part of the curve is behind us. "The remaining devices are mostly ones where paying ESU is cheaper or simpler than replacing whatever they're bolted to. For those, ESU really is the cost of doing business." The Statcounter figures indicate that that "small bump" could be on the way as ESU costs double, but many of the Windows 10 hold outs seem unlikely to be going anywhere just yet. ®

6a5abb7e977bff5b: LONDON, Oct 5 — Disgraced ex-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched a legal challenge over search warrants for his royal homes issued before his February arrest, Britain’s judiciary confirmed Monday, in an unprecedented royal move in modern times.

The force arrested Andrew on his 66th birthday on February 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his links to late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Andrew was released the same day after hours of police questioning, but remained under investigation. He has denied all wrongdoing in his associations with the American financier.
His shock arrest prompted Charles to issue a statement insisting “the law must take its course”.

The Daily Telegraph reported the legal challenge late on Sunday. The newspaper noted it was the first time a member of Britain’s royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
It said his legal team wanted to examine whether the search warrants granted by a judge at London’s Old Bailey court — formally known as the Central Criminal Court — were lawful.
Andrew’s legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
‘Judicial review’

The judiciary’s press office said “the case concerns an application by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor for a judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February 2026”.
Andrew’s arrest and the police searches marked a new low for the ex-prince, who was stripped of his royal titles last year and ousted from his Windsor home over his Epstein connections.
The government has even mulled passing a law to remove him from the line of succession.

Scandal has engulfed the king’s younger brother since one of Epstein’s accusers, Virginia Giuffre, claimed in her posthumous memoirs that she had been trafficked three times to have sex with Andrew when she was a teenager.
The former prince has repeatedly denied the claims. He settled a US civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability.

Epstein emails

Epstein had been convicted in the United States in 2008 of procuring a child for prostitution.

At least nine British police forces confirmed they were looking into claims — some related to Andrew — stemming from the batch of some three million Epstein files released by the US authorities in January.
However, the Thames Valley investigation appears to be the most advanced.

The raid in Windsor lasted six days.
In response to Andrew’s legal challenge, Thames Valley Police said in a statement that its “investigation into misconduct in public office continues”.
“We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained,” it added.
“As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.” — AFP

45e9a7f26a44ce8e: YANGON, Oct 5 — Myanmar warned citizens to expect scheduled power outages starting Monday, saying the electrical grid is being strained by an unseasonable heatwave it blamed on the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Homes and businesses in war-struck Myanmar are regularly plunged into blackouts, some spontaneous and others set on a timetable to ease the burden on the fragile power infrastructure.
Many richer residents use generators or back-up batteries, while the poorer citizens of the tropical nation are left to swelter without fans or air conditioning.
“Due to the effects of severe El Nino conditions, temperatures across the country have risen significantly, resulting in increased electricity consumption,” the energy ministry said.

“To balance electricity consumption with available generation capacity during this period, load management and rotational power distribution will be implemented” starting Monday, said a statement in state media.
El Nino is a natural phenomenon recurring every two to seven years owing to the warming of sea surfaces — bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
Global forecasters predict this year’s event will peak at an intensity never observed in the modern era, compounding the effects of manmade climate change which drives extreme weather patterns.

Myanmar weather officials have warned the country to expect “abnormal rainfalls and storms, drought, extreme heat, drinking water shortage and extreme weather conditions” as a result of the “Super El Nino”.
Late last month the southernmost Tanintharyi Region was lashed by rains which caused widespread flooding and killed at least nine people in a landslide.

Myanmar is currently coming to the end of its wet season, when reservoirs feeding the hydropower plants making up the nation’s largest source of electricity generation are filled by plentiful monsoon rains.
The energy ministry said it was “anticipating more significant depletion of water levels in reservoirs at hydropower plants during the coming dry season” which usually runs from October to May.
In a normal year the coming months are generally some of the coolest of the year in Myanmar, seeing a drop in power demand as citizens turn off fans and air conditioners. — AFP

17c8e8162aa84d6c: There has been much chilly weather in the sunny meadowlands of AI futures. Fortunately, to use an indecently inappropriate adverb, the rest of the world isn’t really looking, being too busy chewing its nails over the very many other intimations of disaster. Sure, rebel swarms of attack agents breaking out of the labs isn’t a good look. OpenAI delaying its IPO and a new model launch likewise. All these things soak up whatever bandwidth the news media have to AI right now. Putting them in a bigger context, that of promises made and not kept, problems known but not fixed, the observable risk-reward ratios as models develop, we may at last start having a sense of what sort of crisis awaits. Actual crises are frequently triggered by crises in confidence, themselves caused when frameworks of assumption stop standing up to reality and wishful thinking. Thus, the assumption to date is that models will get more powerful and infrastructure more capable, in a way that justifies — demands — massive capex. The economics of giant infrastructure investment when you can’t buy what you need is a great bet in free markets that presupposes that freedom, and yeah, about that. A bigger problem is the idea that more powerful AI is always better. It frequently is, but that’s not good enough, When frontier models have to be kept in LLM jail for uncontrollable dishonesty, not so much. Here, the bigger context is that we’ve known that at heart LLM probability space is entirely relative. There is no ground truth there. Nobody has fixed hallucinations, and now we see the fascinating phenomenon of a machine that doesn’t understand truth but can deliberately lie. If more powerful models are better at that, scratch one assumption. Another huge assumption is that even at the current level of model reliability, agentic architectures are ready to be useful. Those who show all the caution of a chronic gambler on a winning "streak" are as ready to get the brakes slammed on as their opposites. The principal contender for the one true proof of concept that agentic AI is a dangerous fount of unexpected consequence is Meta’s new Muse. It is aimed at low-information credulous users and its star turn is, of course, shopping. The AI use case that’s five years away, and always has been. It’s Meta, so of course it soaks up all the information about you, your online activities and the people you talk to as much as it can. It will soon have ultracute animated Tamagotchi-style pets you can wear around your neck to improve your status as a Meta monitoring post. And we did say it was Meta, so has all the attention to security and careful design you may expect. Which is why it’s already been caught sending people’s physical addresses to strangers, and why when researcher Jonny at neuromatch.social went poking around its infrastructure — each instance runs permanently on its own Linux VM — they found just a ton of fun. Headline party tricks hard-coded. What looks like attempts to train off Claude. And yes, you can get it to run your own things on that VM deep within Meta, which Jonny points out is a botnet paradise waiting to happen. This banger of a bad ‘un is being given away to Meta users, who pretty much define a vulnerable target audience for tech that may not be totally trustworthy. Meta, of course, is dead against AI safety regulation. Place your bets on the headlines to follow. In any case, the upside of using agents as demoed in every keynote is either so trivial and trite — book me a restaurant! — or so catastrophic if it fails — organize my family vacation! — that consumer agents are a bust. It’s just that Meta may be bringing a lot of accelerant to that particular fire. There are other fires, of course, many known about since everything kicked off. Model collapse due to training on data contaminated with output? Still a thing, still no fix a "better" AI might provide. And that habit AI has of retailing everything and paying for nothing, choking off its own training data supply chain and a huge chunk of commerce and culture with it? Very much still a thing. Where AI does make consistent progress is in domain-specific tasks. Science, engineering, mathematics, and coding, if you match a model with enough reinforcement learning with humans who know how to manage them, there are startling results. You don’t get much innovation, not much newness, which is the true driver of progress. Better than humans is highly contextual. Computers have been better at chess for decades, but there isn’t a better chess. Horses run faster than humans, and that’s been useful for four millennia, but we got to peak horses quite some time ago. So the question is, have we reached peak AI, where the cost of future developments don’t match the risk they won’t work well enough to justify? If ChatGPT already writes a perfectly good business letter in a couple of seconds, there is no meaningful improvement to be had for users. Most AI is profoundly annoying, in ways that have nothing to do with the models and everything to do with perverted UX in an attempt to justify growth. That is both unsustainable and a tacit admission that AI hasn’t solved its use case problem. If we are at or near peak AI, is that the crisis that bursts that goddam bubble? Certainly a readjustment, as all bets on the continuous uptick curve are off. AI as it stands is useful enough to power a big industry sector, just in ways that are and remain at odds to how it is marketed and its future fantasies. Trust in AI Max may be shaken, but there's still room for lots of improvement. That slowdown that everyone who isn’t a miscreant is calling for may happen organically, if we escape the smoking-is-good-for-you mentality of the Metans and the Muskovites. That’s still a gamble we shouldn't be taking, but the odds may be better than we thought. ®
568b5b5801f65591: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.”

“I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable.
The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now.

On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young.

More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University. In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE.

Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July.

According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot, more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months.
All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on?
It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.

It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up: The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic.

But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible. They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel?

In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search.

With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI, creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years.

And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it.

I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different.
Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: Clarity about what AI can and cannot do and, crucially, a technology that’s not sold as if it’s about to take over the world.
